item.title: AI Literacy as Experimental Practice: Students as Investigators
item.dc:creator: Amarda Shehu, Adonyas Ababu, Asma Akbary, Griffin Allen, Aroush Baig, Tereana Battle, Elias Beall, Christopher Byrom, Matt Dean, Kate Demarco, Ethan Douglass, Luis Granados, Layla Hantush, Andy Hay, Eleanor Hay, Caleb Jackson, Jaewon Jang, Carter Jones, Quanyang Li, Adrian Lopez, Logan Massimo, Garrett McMullin, Ariana Maldonado, Eman Mirza, Hadiya Muddasar, Sara Nuwayhid, Brandon Pak, Ashley Petty, Dryden Rancourt, Lily Rodriguez, Corbin Rogers, Jacob Schiek, Taeseo Seok, Aarav Sethi, Giovanni Vitela, Winston Williams, and Jagan Yetukuri
item.description: Student investigators offer a concrete example of the operationalization of AI literacy as experimental practice.
item.content:encoded:
There is ongoing academic debate on whether one can teach AI literacy to undergraduate students across majors, and if so, how. This article reports a case study: a three-week midterm project embedded in an undergraduate “AI-for-all” course. Students designed reasoning tasks, ran controlled comparisons across widely used chatbots, and evaluated both answer correctness and explanation validity.

Through field experience, students with no STEM background learned what consumer chatbots can and cannot do, documenting systematic brittleness across models that “sounded right but reasoned wrong.” More critically, students built understanding of how to evaluate AI outputs. The midterm gave them agency as investigators rather than passive users. Eager to share their discoveries, they are co-authors of this article. Together, we offer here to educators and the broader scientific community a concrete example of the operationalization of AI literacy as experimental practice. The method, however, is not specific to the classroom. It shows any user how to test an AI system rather than trust it blindly.

The Problem: When Fluency Masks Fragility

A college sophomore asks a chatbot to check her calculus homework. The explanation is articulate and detailed, and the final answer matches the back of the textbook. She submits with confidence. Later, when reviewing with a teaching assistant, she realizes that three intermediate steps violate basic algebra. Consumer chatbots now output answers alongside explanations that read as instruction, with the tone and structure of a human teacher.11 The form is pedagogically persuasive and so becomes an implicit signal of reliability. Telling students “do not trust AI” is ineffective; 86% of them report already using AI in their studies, with 89% of those using it specifically for homework.3 Explaining that these systems operate as probabilistic predictors may be conceptually true, but it does not reliably translate into verification behavior. Students can define “hallucination” on an exam10 and still accept a confident response in the moment, particularly when the response includes a plausible narrative of reasoning. Knowing that a system can be wrong is not the same as being able to detect when it is wrong, to explain why it is wrong, and to recognize when a correct answer is accompanied by an invalid rationale. In a world where explanations are part of the product form, AI literacy must include disciplined habits of checking, not only conceptual vocabulary.

Our approach: A case study in teaching evaluation. This article reports a case study: a midterm project embedded in UNIV 182, an undergraduate “AI-for-all” course at George Mason University designed by Shehu for students across majors with no assumed STEM background. The midterm asked student teams to design reasoning tests for consumer chatbots and to evaluate two distinct outcomes: answer correctness, and explanation validity. This separation forced students to practice a distinction rarely made in everyday use. Over three weeks, students working in teams created more than 100 original prompts spanning reasoning families, ran each prompt across four chatbots, and documented more than 320 responses with follow-up explanations when needed. The assignment was simultaneously an assessment of course learning and a guided apprenticeship in experimental design, measurement, and disciplined skepticism.

What this Practice article offers.  We describe the midterm as a replicable instructional design: the reasoning-task taxonomy, a compact exemplar signaling the prompt-design space, and a controlled protocol separating answer correctness from explanation validity. We report what emerged when teams applied that protocol, using quantitative summaries and vignettes to illustrate how chatbot explanation fluency can diverge from valid constraint following. We show how the assessment functioned as discovery through AI Studios, evidence trails, and scoring reconciliation, and then close with a practical replication guide. Because students carried out the investigation and wanted to share their artifacts publicly, they appear as co-investigators and co-authors.

The Assignment: Three Weeks, Ten Prompts, Four Chatbots

The core challenge.  The midterm began with a question frequently heard in public discourse: Can consumer chatbots “reason?” The course reframed this as a design problem: If you wanted to test it systematically, what would you do, and how would you justify your conclusions? Each team of three to five students authored 10 prompts and ran them across four consumer chatbots. For every response, teams recorded the verbatim interaction and evaluated two separate constructs: whether the final answer was correct, and whether the explanation was valid. Answer correctness is familiar to students because it resembles ordinary grading. Explanation validity is the harder half. Students are told to show their work, but they are rarely asked to judge whether the work is valid. Doing so requires the evaluator to check whether intermediate steps follow stated rules, maintain internal consistency, and actually support the output claim.

Why a chatbot-reasoning midterm?  Midsemester is an effective checkpoint for asking students to synthesize conceptual understanding. By this point in UNIV 182, students had encountered core ideas about learning from data, evaluation and bias, common failure modes, and the basic architecture that leads to contemporary LLM chatbots, including the distinction between a base language model and a policy-aligned conversational system. The midterm, therefore, used the public question “Can these chatbots reason?” as an integrative vehicle for three competencies: experimental design under constraints, separation of outcome from justification, and critical AI literacy as practice.

A practical reasoning taxonomy.  Because most students in UNIV 182 are new to experimental design, the instructor provided a lightweight taxonomy of reasoning task families as a shared vocabulary to help teams diversify prompt sets, avoid mistaking a single successful interaction for general capability, and describe what a prompt was demanding. The project specifications defined six classes: pattern completion, transformation rules, spatial and visual reasoning, computation under simple constraints, relational and logical reasoning, and analogical reasoning, with examples for each in the supplementary appendix,a available with this article in the ACM Digital Library. These families were inspired by the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) benchmark,1 but the course treated reasoning as a design space rather than directing students to ARC. Students had to operationalize the taxonomy to construct varied, scorable prompt sets without assuming any particular overlap between ARC and any model’s training data. In practice, the taxonomy also served as a common language for articulating failure modes, for example “right answer, wrong rationale,” and sensitivity to small constraint changes.

An example that opens a design space.  The midterm specification included an exemplar of a diagnostic reasoning probe: “ABCD → ABCE. Following the same rule, what should OOPPQQRR become?” The prompt appears almost trivial at first glance, but it was designed to show how a simple transfer question can elicit qualitatively different behaviors once a chatbot must infer an implicit rule, apply it to a structurally different input, and defend the result with an explanation. In classroom discussion, the exemplar served as a concrete invitation into a broader design space by illustrating how task demands can be varied without making the problem mathematically advanced, since the first instance establishes an implied rule, and the second tests whether the system generalizes that rule rather than improvises a new one. The instructor provided a sample interaction with Grok 4 and used guiding questions, such as “What is the system doing here?”, “Would you consider this an explanation?”, and “How would you rate the validity of the explanation?” to demonstrate what the midterm required: observation, argument, and scoring.

A controlled comparison protocol.  To keep experiments interpretable, teams were required to hold inputs constant across systems. Each prompt had to be submitted to all four chatbots using the same wording. When a chatbot produced an answer without an explanation, students followed up with a standard request for reasoning,11 so explanation validity could be scored.8 Teams documented the complete interaction, including any follow-up turns, and recorded scores for both answer correctness and explanation validity on a 0–100 scale with a written justification.

Deliverables and in-class studios.  Teams submitted a brief written report and a short slide presentation using templates provided by the instructor. The report included the prompt set, raw interaction log, scores, and a rationale for each score, while the presentation required teams to communicate their main observations concisely and to include explicit caveats about what their evidence did and did not support. Together, these deliverables enforced a provenance trail from claim to evidence to interpretation and gave students practice in defending conclusions from observation. The project was further supported through in-class “AI Studios,” extended work sessions in which teams drafted prompts, tested early variants, and calibrated scoring while the instructor circulated, providing immediate feedback on whether a prompt was too familiar, too ambiguous to score, or genuinely revealing, as well as guidance on what should count as a valid explanation and how to handle partial correctness.

Why teams were essential.  Team-based work made the workload feasible and created opportunities for productive disagreement. Students frequently debated whether an explanation actually followed the prompt semantics, whether a model had introduced an unstated assumption, or whether a partial score was warranted. Those debates were not a side effect. They were part of the learning outcomes, because they pushed students toward explicit criteria and evidence-based reconciliation.

Consent, privacy, and data stewardship.  Because the midterm produces artifacts that can outlive the course, consent and data handling were built into the design. Student co-authors provided explicit, opt-in consent collected separately from grading to reduce coercion risk. They were also informed about the long-term implications of public authorship and that co-authorship was not required for course credit. While teams submitted raw interaction logs as part of the course deliverables, we report only aggregated patterns and representative excerpts, not complete logs, to reduce privacy risk. Accordingly, the quantitative results should be interpreted as descriptive summaries of classroom evidence rather than claims of chatbot superiority, since a single course-based case study cannot support broad ranking conclusions. The George Mason University Institutional Review Board reviewed this work and determined that it qualifies for exemption under 45 CFR 46.104(d), Category 4 (STUDY00001028, determined Mar. 11, 2026).

What Students Found

Eleven teams completed the assignment; ten reported standardized numeric scores that enabled aggregation across teams. Each team tested more than 10b prompts of its own design across chatbots, producing the per-team landscape shown in Table 1. For aggregate reporting, we defined a Quantitative Core (QC) after submissions were received: the subset of teams that scored both answer correctness and explanation validity on a comparable set of chatbots. Teams that reported only qualitative findings, omitted one of the two metrics, or substituted an alternative system (e.g., Team One substituting Gemini for Claude) are preserved in Table 1 for transparency but excluded from the relevant column of Table 2 to avoid imputation or rubric retrofitting. Table 2 summarizes QC performance by chatbot as an unweighted mean across eligible teams for each metric, and reports the number of contributing teams explicitly because the effective sample size differs by chatbot and metric. Dispersion across teams is included intentionally, since variance is itself part of what the assignment teaches. Figure 1 provides a visual summary. The central point is not that one system “wins” but rather that even in a short, student-designed probe set, the relationship between answer correctness and explanation validity is not guaranteed, and performance is sensitive to prompt design and scoring criteria.

Student teams repeatedly observed gaps between answer correctness and explanation validity. In many cases, a model produced the correct answer while offering a justification that violated the stated rules, skipped necessary steps, or introduced assumptions not specified by the prompt. In other cases, a model offered an explanation that was internally coherent but ended in an incorrect answer. This distinction was important because the assignment required separate scoring. Explanation validity moved from an abstract concern about “hallucination” to a concrete evaluation target.

Students generally found that short, highly familiar tasks were less diagnostic. Chatbots often performed well on straightforward arithmetic; simple sequences; and prompts with explicit, common rules.2 In class, this became a design lesson. When early trials produced near-perfect scores, teams were prompted to revise toward prompts that required longer state tracking, interacting constraints, or less canonical surface forms. Prompts became most diagnostic, particularly in spatial descriptions and multi-step transformations.9 Students documented recurring behaviors in those settings: skipping a stated rule, silently adding a new rule, producing an overconfident answer that did not match the intermediate steps, or giving an explanation that described one procedure while actually executing another. Several teams reported that format shifts, including emoji-based variants of the same underlying rule, could change outcomes in ways that surprised them. A useful meta-observation emerged in studio: Once students realized that the goal was not to “trick” a chatbot (though this was a self-reported great motivation for many students) but to reveal a limitation with evidence, reasoning tasks became more complex and creative.

What “failure” looked like: Six discovery moments.  Across teams, conclusions converged on the following: “Consumer chatbots can often perform well on short, structured tasks with explicit rules but are brittle on tasks requiring spatial simulation, multi-step transformations, strict constraint tracking, or generalization under format shifts.” Several teams characterized chatbot behavior as “imitation of reasoning:” plausible narratives plus partial rule-following, without consistent reliability across diverse problem types. Students learned how to ask disciplined questions and communicate evidence-based interpretations with appropriate caveats.

The following vignettes capture key student observations and connect them to specific literacy lessons.

Fluent Introspection without Convergence

Claude’s “Thinking Voice.” One team reported that Claude 4 often began with a high-confidence “I got this” posture, then shifted into uncertainty while producing long, human-like “thinking” text (“Let me try this … oh, that is not right”). Students interpreted this as simulated deliberation: the model producing a convincing process narrative even when not converging on a correct solution.

Pedagogical impact. Students learned that an internal-looking monologue is not evidence of correct computation. Verbosity substituted for constraint tracking creates cognitive load on the user without reliability.

“Fighting with Itself” as an Observable Behavior

Grok’s iterative “self-disagreement.” Another team reported models declaring the answer incorrect, then repeating the same reasoning process many times without resolving the underlying mistake. Students described this as “fighting with itself” to capture the generation of signals of self-correction with no corrective updates.

Pedagogical impact. Students learned to distinguish meta-level signals (“I am uncertain”) from object-level correction (changing flawed steps).

Overcomplication and Signal Loss

When more context hurt. One team reported that as more prompts, and therefore more total interaction context, were introduced, answer accuracy and explanation quality decreased, particularly for ChatGPT and Perplexity.

Pedagogical impact. Students learned that additional context is not always additional signal,9 and longer interactions can introduce new opportunities for misinterpretation.

Rules vs. Generalization

Pattern followers, not reliable general thinkers. One team summarized a takeaway succinctly: The models they tested were “good pattern followers, not reliable general thinkers,” and “users cannot trust confidence or nice wording as proof the reasoning is correct,” a conclusion they grounded in multiple instances where a model restated a rule correctly but executed it incorrectly on a close variant, succeeded in one representation but failed in another (e.g., when the same rule was expressed with emojis), or produced a correct answer through a shortcut but could not justify it under the prompt’s intended semantics.

Pedagogical impact. Students learned to shift from consuming chatbot outputs to evaluating systems, treating fluent explanations as hypotheses to verify and prioritizing reproducible evidence over confident phrasing.

Sounding Right while Reasoning Wrong

Transformation rules and a signature failure mode. Teams documented a recurring pattern on transformation-rule prompts. A model sometimes produced a correct final answer while offering an explanation of the form “I applied the rule by …” that did not actually match the stated transformation. Students noted that the explanation was fluent and confident but violated a constraint that was explicit in the prompt. As one team put it, “If we had not checked, we would have trusted it.”

Pedagogical impact. Students learned that chatbots may violate explicit constraints in their reasoning, their final answer, or both, and that fluent explanations must be verified against the prompt’s stated rules.

Context Richness as Mediator of “Apparent Reasoning”

When prompt structure drives perceived reasoning. One team concluded that apparent chatbot reasoning was highly dependent on the clarity and structure of context in the prompt. When context was rich and organized, the models produced more accurate answers and more coherent explanations. When prompts were vague, the models drifted into assumptions or over-analysis.

Pedagogical impact. Students learned that apparent “reasoning” is often mediated by prompt structure, with rich, well-organized context reducing drift and unstated assumptions, and that treating context design as experimental control helps distinguish framing effects from stable capability.

The Double Duty: Assessment Becomes Discovery

From “AI as magic” to “AI as testable artifact.”  Many undergraduates first encounter chatbots as high-agency assistants that produce fluent text on demand. In that posture, it is natural to treat the output as an authority and to treat the explanation as evidence that the system “understands.” The midterm was designed to interrupt that default stance. Students were asked to treat chatbot outputs as claims that require evaluation and to treat the system itself as a testable artifact. Three design choices made that stance shift. First, students authored the probes. That requirement made it clear that “reasoning” is not a single capability but a family of behaviors that can be stressed in different ways. Second, students ran controlled comparisons by holding prompts constant across systems, which discouraged one-off anecdotes and made differences salient. Third, students evaluated both outputs and explanations, which created repeated opportunities to notice a signature failure mode that novice users otherwise miss: a correct answer accompanied by an invalid rationale, or a fluent rationale that does not support the answer.

What students learned by measuring “reasoning.”  The assignment forced students to operationalize an ambiguous public question—“Can chatbots reason?”—into measurable proxies. Three lessons recurred across teams:

  1. Reasoning is plural—The category scaffold functioned as a practical taxonomy: A system could appear strong in one family of tasks and brittle in another. This mattered pedagogically because it countered two common but opposing misconceptions, namely that a chatbot can do everything and that it can do nothing. Students learned to make conditional claims tied to task demands.

  2. The correct answers can be achieved for invalid reasons—Separating answer correctness from explanation validity required students to define what counts as valid justification, including rule compliance, internal consistency, and alignment between intermediate steps and the final claim. This is transferable literacy. Many real-world harms arise not from a wrong answer in isolation, but from an invalid explanation that gets trusted, repeated, and embedded into subsequent decisions.

  3. Prompt design is part of the phenomenon—Minor changes in wording, specificity, or constraint clarity could alter both answers and explanations. Rather than treating this as a nuisance, the assignment treated it as central to real-world reliability, because end users control prompts. Students began to view prompt structure as experimental control and to interpret sensitivity as an empirical property worth documenting.

How “AI Studios” and teams made methodology visible.  Extended in-class work sessions, which we called AI Studios, were essential to making abstract expectations concrete. Studios provided protected time for diverse-background students to make progress on technical work without requiring extensive prior experience and made quality criteria visible through immediate feedback on prompt design and scoring rationales. Studios also normalized iteration as the core learning loop. Team-based work turned this into a small-scale research workflow, with students delegating systems, running parallel trials, and reconciling logs in shared documents. This structure produced practical lessons about reproducibility and why scientific claims about AI require protocols and explicit criteria. The presentation then required students to distill technical work into structured arguments with quantitative summaries, qualitative examples, and appropriate caveats. In that sense, the midterm functioned as learning disguised as assessment by requiring students to do evaluation rather than merely learn about evaluation.

Failure modes as teachable moments.  Students encountered failure modes that map directly to trust calibration in everyday use. In some cases, a chatbot defended an incorrect path with high confidence, elaborating without resolving contradictions. In other cases, it introduced extra assumptions or invented rules not present in the prompt. Students learned to classify this as constraint violation, not as creativity, which is precisely the distinction that matters in decision-support contexts. At least one team also labeled a model’s tendency to shift answers under user pressure as sycophancy5,6,7 and treated that behavior as evidence against robust truth-tracking when the user is confident but wrong. The instructional payoff was concrete. Students stopped treating “helpfulness” and verbosity as evidence of correctness. They began to look for alignment between the prompt, the steps, and the claim.

Replication Guide: Running This in Your Course

Timeline and structure.  We ran the project over three weeks, with each week anchored by an AI Studio session that provided protected time for design and calibration. Table 3 provides the week-by-week timeline.

What is essential.  We identify five components as difficult to remove without changing the pedagogical function of the assignment:

  1. The separation of answer correctness and explanation validity, which forces the conceptual distinction that most novice users do not make

  2. Controlled comparison, meaning the same prompt is submitted to multiple systems so students can see differences without confounds

  3. Evidence trail, as students must document verbatim prompts, outputs, and follow-up turns so claims can be traced back to data

  4. Team structure, which makes the workload feasible and generates productive inter-rater disagreement that must be resolved with criteria

  5. In-class work time, which is where methodology becomes visible, and where non-technical students learn how to iterate from a weak prompt to a strong diagnostic probe

What can be adapted?  Several parameters can be adjusted without losing the core learning loop. The number of prompts can be reduced for shorter courses or expanded for more time. The number of chatbots can vary based on availability. The taxonomy should remain a scaffold, but the instructor can emphasize different categories depending on course (learning) outcomes.c The scoring scale can be simplified if needed, provided the separation of answer and explanation remains. Deliverables can also change, as long as students are required to present a provenance trail and to communicate caveats.

Resources and requirements.  The project can be run using free consumer-access tiers for common chatbots, along with ordinary collaboration tools such as shared documents for logging and analysis; at our institution, students have access to an internal file-sharing platform. It is worth noting that the main resource to provide to students is instructor availability during studios for immediate feedback on prompt design and scoring criteria. In our setting, three to four studio sessions of 60 to 75 minutes (the course ran twice weekly, with each session limited to 75 minutes) were sufficient to keep teams aligned and progressing.

Handling scoring and disagreement.  Teams may initially struggle with a question that is central to the learning objective: what counts as a valid explanation. We recommend starting Week 1 with a brief calibration exercise built around a shared exemplar. The instructor used the ABCD → ABCE task for this purpose: The class scored a sample chatbot interaction together so three criteria were made explicit before teams drafted their own rubrics, namely rule compliance (does the explanation follow the prompt constraints?), internal consistency (do the steps cohere with one another?), and alignment (do the stated steps produce the final answer?). Studios in Weeks 1 and 2 kept these criteria visible as teams encountered ambiguous cases in their own logs, for example, partial credit for a single violated step. In Week 3, members who had scored the same interaction differently returned to the prompt text, cited the specific intermediate step at issue, and revised scores when a criterion violation could be demonstrated; teams varied in whether they assigned a single scorer per chatbot or used multiple raters, so we treat the resulting scores as student-annotated classroom measurements rather than benchmark labels, and we note formal inter-rater checks as a direction for subsequent offerings of the course. Reasonable disagreement is acceptable when documented and justified. In practice, students learn as much from the debate as from the score.

Common challenges and practical solutions.  Table 4 lists implementation challenges that arose repeatedly and the practical interventions that resolved them.

Success markers.  The assignment is working when students debate whether an explanation is valid rather than stopping at answer correctness, when teams revise prompts based on early trials, when reports include explicit caveats about ambiguity or scoring uncertainty, and when presentations prioritize surprising behaviors and evidence over rankings. The clearest signal is transfer: Students begin to articulate how they would verify explanations in everyday use.

Adapting for different contexts.  In a shorter course, the scope can be reduced through fewer prompts and fewer systems. For technical majors, instructors can require a prompt sensitivity analysis through controlled paraphrases and stability checks. For large classes, a shared prompt pool from which teams select and refine a subset preserves student design while improving comparability. In asynchronous or online formats, studio sessions can be replaced with peer critique, where teams post prompts and receive comments on clarity, diagnostic value, and scorability. Finally, by the time this article is read, the consumer chatbot landscape will likely have changed. Three points of practical advice follow for instructors interested in replicating this midterm. The specific systems matter less than picking four contemporaneous, accessible chatbots of broadly comparable capability; the exercise works with any such set. Refusals and policy-shaped outputs may be more common than in our window and can be scored as data rather than treated as broken trials, since they are part of what end users encounter. Chatbots may also offer additional modes, including thinking, research, Web access, and persistent memory; instructors should decide before Week 1 whether to run with defaults on or off and apply that choice consistently across the selected systems.

Implications and Conclusion: Evaluation as Classroom Practice

This article began with a pedagogical challenge: Students are using consumer chatbots but most lack a framework for judging when a fluent explanation is reliable and when it is not. Our response in UNIV 182 was to treat chatbots as empirical objects of study and to position students as investigators rather than consumers.

Over three weeks, students with no assumed STEM background designed sets of reasoning prompts, ran controlled comparisons across widely used chatbots, and evaluated both answer correctness and explanation validity. Seen as assessment, the project offers a pragmatic alternative in which chatbots are treated as objects of analysis and become a material for learning. Students are assessed on whether they can construct a defensible test, document the trail from prompt to output to score, and communicate caveats. The focus shifts from whether AI was used to whether AI was evaluated responsibly. Seen as a complement to benchmark-style evaluation, the project highlights interactional features that shape trust in everyday use. In classroom data, the most consequential issues were not limited to wrong answers. They included explanations that sounded instructional while violating constraints, and behaviors in which a system elaborated rather than revised when challenged. For end users, reliability includes stability under paraphrase, restated constraints, and minor format changes.

We close with a warning, a limitation, and an opportunity. The warning is that access conditions are part of what an instructor must manage. Our comparisons used free consumer tiers, and students should not feel pressured to purchase paid subscriptions to participate or to obtain “better” results.

The limitation is that this is a pedagogical intervention with empirical byproducts, not a controlled benchmark study. The assignment specified in advance what every team would follow: the taxonomy, the separation of answer correctness and explanation validity, the controlled-comparison protocol, and the studio and consent structures. Teams authored different prompts, applied slightly different rubrics, and interacted with evolving consumer interfaces, so aggregate numbers should be read as descriptive summaries rather than definitive rankings. Two analytic choices were made after submissions, the Quantitative Core used for aggregation and the vignette grouping of student observations.

The opportunity, and the contribution we hope this case study makes, is a replicable pathway to AI literacy as experimental classroom practice. It is worth noting that the opportunity reaches beyond the classroom. Credulity is the path of least resistance, and the same practice we have related in this article teaches any user to resist it; to test an AI system rather than accept what it says, and to learn what it can do by finding where it breaks and by how much. Confident, fluent nonsense is an old human craft that AI now can produce at scale. The work presented here teaches anyone to catch it and to judge whether these systems can be trusted where the stakes are real.

item.title: Combining Tests and Proofs with Contracts for Better Software Verification
item.dc:creator: Li Huang, Bertrand Meyer, and Manuel Oriol
item.description: One can treat program proofs and dynamic tests to verify program correctness as complementary rather than exclusive.
item.content:encoded:
Software development is not just an intellectual exercise; it is also an engineering endeavor, with considerable benefits when it succeeds and the risk of considerable damage if done incorrectly. Software verification seeks to avoid such adverse outcomes. It has two variants: dynamic and static. Dynamic verification, also known as testing, consists of executing a system on sample input conditions and checking the results against expected properties (“oracles”). For many projects in industry, testing is the only form of verification. In contrast, verification among programming researchers usually refers to static methods, which do not execute the program but rather analyze its text, usually in its source form. The analysis may be directed toward specific properties or it may perform a full proof of correctness, which requires a formal specification of the program’s intended behavior, against which its actual behavior can be assessed.

Key Insights

  • Software verification is too important and challenging to justify excluding any approach that can help. Both static approaches (proofs) and dynamic ones (tests) have their place. Each compensates for the other’s limitations.

  • Combining them makes it possible to turn a failed proof attempt into a failed test, immediately providing a clue as to what is wrong. Other applications include automatic generation of 100%-coverage test suites, automatic generation of guaranteed-correct bug fixes, better tests for programs with loops, and validation of the MC/DC test standard.

  • This work and the underlying AutoProof framework take advantage of contracts: specifications embedded in the code, as found in Eiffel.

There is a long history of pitting tests against proofs. Practitioners often reject proofs as too difficult, costly, and impractical. Critics of testing, for their part, dismiss tests as ineffective since they exercise only a minuscule subset of all possible cases; as famously stated by Dijkstra, “Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!”11 The controversy has been at times heated, with strong dismissals of proofs15 (against Naur’s proof attempts),10,33 and equally harsh statements about the limitations of testing by proponents of proofs.

In recent years, more conciliatory attitudes have emerged, attested to by (among other developments) the creation of the Tests and Proofs (TAP) conference, running since 2007. Verification is difficult in any of its forms, and should not let dogma exclude any potentially useful technique. Even the staunchest proof advocate must accept that it may not be possible to specify all properties formally, particularly “non-functional” attributes such as performance and fault tolerance, and that the value of any proof is conditional on the assumption that both the compiler and hardware preserve program semantics, leaving room for tests. One may also note the role of failures on both sides:

  • A failed test is actually a proof: It demonstrates that the program is incorrect—in the same way that in the Popperian view of science a negative experiment proves the theory wrong. (In this respect, one may interpret Dijkstra’s quip, usually heard as an indictment of tests, as an advertisement for them: It is one of the goals of software verification to help uncover faults.)

  • A failed proof attempt often leaves us clueless as to what is wrong. To understand, it is useful to see a test triggering the underlying fault, if any. This idea will be developed in a later section.

Test-and-proof complementarity goes beyond these observations. The catalyst for the work discussed here is a feature found in modern program-proving tools, such as those based on satisfiability modulo theories (SMT),2 that tries to generate counterexamples that violate the specification. A proof will succeed if it cannot produce any; but for an incorrect program, the counterexamples yield tests. We may also use the resulting information to propose corrections to bugs. And for a correct program, we may obtain a regression test suite by injecting faults and producing counterexamples.

We have applied these ideas to develop verification and program-repair techniques that exploit this complementarity, while taking advantage of the design by contract approach to software construction.28 Until now, the steps in this process have been described in separate articles;18,23  here, we provide a comprehensive and up-to-date presentation of them for a broader audience. First, we explain the general idea: taking advantage of the information associated with proof failures. Then we review design by contract, a key ingredient of the approach. In subsequent sections, we introduce successive refinements of the basic idea:

  • Proof2Test18 turns failed proofs, often seemingly unhelpful, into useful test cases, which offer concrete evidence of why the proofs fail, enabling programmers to understand and address the underlying issues.

  • Proof2Fix19 extends the combination of tests and proofs to automatic program repair by providing a guaranteed validation of fixes through the prover.

  • Seeding contradiction21 (SC) extends the capability to systematic test generation. By deliberately creating failed proofs and running them through Proof2Test, it can produce a collection of tests that satisfy code-coverage criteria. It also incorporates loop unrolling to create tests that explore loop behavior and helps provide an assessment of modified condition/decision coverage (MC/DC), a testing criterion sometimes viewed skeptically but widely used in industry.

In the final sections, we review earlier work on neighboring topics and draw conclusions.

The Core Idea: Proofs and Their Failures

The idea of proving programs correct (already prefigured in visionary late-1940s articles by Turing and Von Neumann) goes back to the seminal work of Floyd, Hoare, Dijkstra, McCarthy, Naur, and others in the 1970s and 1980s. What has changed in recent years is the appearance of practical tools—“provers”—that can prove the correctness of programs, including large ones. Proving a significant program involves far too many steps to make human checking either practical or (if it somehow were possible) believable. Consequently, the role of automation has been essential. Although still used by only a minority of projects, provers have achieved some industry successes.17

A prover works on the combination of a program and a specification (often expressed as “contracts,” explained in the next section). The starting point for the present work is to take advantage of the technique used internally by many modern provers: to seek one or more “counterexamples”—example inputs falsifying the expected properties. If this attempt fails, the proof succeeds.a The focus is on the intermediate steps when the proof fails—meaning the search for a counterexample succeeds—and, more specifically, on the counterexamples themselves.

Successive developments show that this idea has several fruitful applications. The first is to turn counterexamples into tests. A proof failure is disconcerting: “Postcondition violated” does not help the programmer understand what has been done wrong. Internally, though, the prover has a counterexample; “For input 5, the output is -3 while required to be positive” is considerably more informative for a programmer, even more so if accompanied by an automatically generated runnable test reproducing the failure. In other words, a tool can turn failed proofs into failed tests, with two major benefits: providing concrete, runnable evidence to the programmer; and yielding a regression test to be run again in the later history of the project once the bug has been fixed. Those are the functions of Proof2Test.

The next application is to use the counterexamples to generate program fixes. Automatic program repair (APR) needs “invariants” characterizing failed executions. Instead of getting them from manually generated tests, the present approach can generate guaranteed invariants; instead of validating fixes through tests, it can guarantee their correctness by running them through the prover. Those are the functions of Proof2Fix.

For critical systems, the test suite must reach a high level of coverage, going beyond basic “branch coverage” to such industry-standard measures as MC/DC, and unfolding loops so that the tests can exercise several successive iterations rather than just zero or one.

The Role of Contracts

While of general applicability, the results reported here rely on a contract mechanism, offered by various languages including the one used here, Eiffel. Contracts are needed because verifying the correctness of a program requires having a specification of its intended behavior. Contracts are elements of specification that are embedded in the code itself (rather than in separate documents) and, as a result, can be used for both testing (which will evaluate them in test runs) and proofs. They appear in several modes:

  • Simple assertions (check, in Figure 5): properties that must hold at specific points in the code

  • Preconditions (require, lines 5–6 in Figure 2): properties that clients must satisfy for any call

  • Postconditions (ensure, lines 27–29 in Figure 2): properties that the routine (supplier) guarantees

  • Loop invariants (invariant, lines 13–16 in Figure 2): properties guaranteed after loop initialization and every iteration

  • Loop variants (variant, lines 24–25 in Figure 2): integer measures that remain non-negative and decrease at each loop iteration, ensuring loop termination

As an example, Figure 2 shows an Eiffel class MAX. The intent of the max function is to return into Result the maximum element of an integer array a of size a.count. The postcondition clauses in lines 28 and 29 (is_max and in_array) specify the intent of the function: Every element of the array should be less than or equal to Result; and at least one element should be equal to Result.

Contracts are a strong enabler for both testing and proving because they are specification elements embedded in the code itself. For testing, they make it possible to identify the source of a bug precisely: A precondition violation indicates a bug in the client; if the test passed the precondition, any subsequent failure is a bug in the code of the supplier method. Tools such as AutoTest29 have used these ideas to provide automated random testing. For proving, most tools rely on Dijkstra’s weakest-precondition (wp) calculus,12 which deliver their full potential when the code already includes postconditions and explicit loop variants and invariants.

Many programming languages (e.g., Java, C#, C++, and Python) support simple assertions but have no specific constructs for the other uses listed above. Extensions to some of them have introduced such constructs, for example, JML9 for Java and Spec# for C#. A handful of languages, however, enjoy built-in contract mechanisms. These include Eiffel, SPARK, Dafny, and the upcoming “C++26” ISO/IEC C++ standard. The present work is based on Eiffel because of its extensive support for contracts as a core native mechanism rather than as an add-on, its practical availability through tools such as the EiffelStudio compiler and IDE, and its experience with research on tools using contracts for automatic test generation (AutoTest), automatic program repair (AutoFix), and proofs (AutoProof, used in the toolset presented below).29,38,39 All of the tools and techniques described in this article have been integrated into the research version of EiffelStudio (Figure 1).

Contracts are also necessary to apply the theory used by many modern provers: “Hoare logic,” of which Dijkstra’s weakest-precondition (wp) calculus12 is a variant. The basic condition to be established for a routine r of body b, precondition P, and postcondition Q is:

P ⇒ ( b wp Q )

where b wp Q is the the weakest possible assertion such that b, started in a state satisfying P, will terminate in a state satisfying Q. The prover will compute this condition for every r and then prove that every call satisfies it. As discussed in the next section, provers based on SMT solving achieve this goal by trying to find an assignment of variables (a counterexample) that contradicts it. The proof succeeds if they cannot. The present work exploits the converse case.

Creating Tests from Failed Proofs

The observations of the previous section highlight what a failure means in the proving and testing processes, and how the two cases relate to each other. A failed proof leaves the programmer wondering what is wrong. A failed test provides concrete evidence.

For anyone trying to prove a program correct, failure is a familiar companion. Textbooks usually show successful proofs, but in practice the path to success can be frustrating. For example, say you are using a prover and prepared the next proof step diligently: the program, its specification (contracts), and extra annotations known as verification conditions. You click “Verify” and the prover tells you it is not able to perform the proof successfully. Figure 2 shows such a response, for the AutoProof prover, before the inclusion of the tools discussed below.

Where does one go from here? The message states that a postcondition (line 28), describing the intended effect of the routine is_max, may be violated. That does not even mean that the routine is incorrect, just that the prover cannot prove that it is correct. Is the implementation wrong (the most frequent case)? Is the specification wrong? Did the developer forget to include some verification conditions? Or does the task exceed the prover’s abilities?

The process of getting to a successful proof has sometimes been called static debugging, in contrast to the classical form of debugging, which is dynamic, as it involves running the program on tests. When they succeed, static techniques provide a guarantee of correctness that no set of tests can match. But a failed test has the practical advantage of giving the programmer directly useful evidence of what is wrong, helping to identify the source of the failure—the bug (fault)—and correcting it. Such responses are known in the psychology literature as constructive feedback,24 although the basic idea is clear from everyday experience (“Your answer is wrong” is less effective than “On page 3 you mistook pounds for kilograms”). In dealing with programming errors, the programmer needs to mentally reproduce the faulty program’s execution. A failed test provides such a directly usable indication; the failed-proof message in Figure 2 does not.

Modern proof tools have the potential to tell us more. To establish Hoare-style properties as discussed in the previous section, AutoProof relies on Boogie,26 which itself uses an “SMT solver” such as Z3,2 whose method to prove a property consists of looking for counterexamples that defeat it. The proof succeeds when it cannot find any. It fails if it finds one or more. To gain more concrete information, the programmer could then in principle explore the solver’s internals for counterexamples. Often, however, that information is spread over hundreds of lines in internal files whose format, SMT-LIB,2 is intended for verification experts. Tools such as Boogie Verification Debugger (BVD) and Boogaloo can help, but remain largely static.

Proof2Test18 extends AutoProof and provides the missing step. It analyzes internal information to display a directly understandable input example of what caused the failure, consisting here of the array’s size and some of its elements (Figure 3a), and then generates a test case (Figure 3b).

In Figure 3a, the values are small: a two-element array with values 0 and 1. If asked to produce one counterexample, the SMT solver typically yields much larger values. Here, it initially produces an array size a.count of 11,800 and values a [11799] = 0 and a [11800] = 5. For disproof purposes (showing that the postcondition does not hold), they are as good as any others. Since the purpose of Proof2Test is to provide concrete evidence that helps programmers figure out concretely what is going on, we prefer values that mean something at the human scale. Proof2Test takes advantage of the underlying prover’s ability to generate not just one but several counterexamples (when provided with different seeds). It applies a minimization algorithm20 to generate successive ones until it finds minimal values, such as those in Figure 3. As with traditional programmer-devised test cases, they enable the programmer to relate to the failure by trying them out, as shown in Figure 2, and to see that on loop initialization at lines 10–12, Result = 0 and i = 2 so that at line 18 the exit condition evaluates to True, terminating the loop and revealing the fault: Early termination prevents the program from getting to the maximum value at position 2. To eliminate the error, it suffices to strengthen the exit condition to permit one more loop iteration: Change i ≥ a.count to i > a.count.

In addition to producing information that helps programmers understand and correct the fault behind a failure, Proof2Test can turn the counterexample into a test. Figure 3b is actually an executable test case produced by Proof2Test, expressed in the programming language. Programmers can run the test and observe, step by step, how it breaks the specification:

  • Create an instance current_object of class MAX (line 7).

  • Create an integer array a and fill it with values 0 at position 1 and 1 at index 2 (lines 8–9).

  • Call the erroneous function max on current_object with a as argument (line 10).

Running this code in AutoTest produces a runtime failure from the violation of the postcondition is_max, providing tangible evidence (not available from the failed proof attempt) of what is wrong with the version in Figure 2 and making it possible to resume the development process.

A preliminary evaluation of Proof2Test on 20 Eiffel programs18 demonstrated the approach’s potential. With an Intel 12-core processor and 32GB of RAM, the above process takes less than 0.5 seconds on average. In most cases, the generated failing test is useful: Executing it yields a specific trace illustrating how the program leads to the same contract violation that makes the proof fail; programmers can use the debugger’s step-by-step mode to understand the issue.

In a small proportion of cases, the generated test does not lead to a failure. The reason is usually that the implementation is “correct” in some intuitive sense—it does what the programmer somehow intended—but the specification is incomplete. These passing test runs are useful too, although in a different way from the failing ones: They alert the developers to a problem in the specification. (We can hardly say that a program is correct if we are not able to state precisely what it is supposed to do.) In either case, the generated tests are important as regression tests. Once the bugs have been corrected, every previously failing test should become part of the project’s regression suite.

Experiment results20 also show that minimization is cost-effective: In most cases, it reduces the values of integer variables by more than 80%, with an average cost of less than four extra reverification runs. Most minimized values are small and relatable: Out of 125, 108 are in the range [-2, 2], out of which 58 are zero; others are usually close to some constants appearing in the program.

Combining Tests and Proofs for Better Program Repair

Identifying bugs is good; correcting them is better. Automatic program repair (APR) has demonstrated its potential in producing useful fixes. The Achilles’ heel of most existing APR approaches31 is that they rely on test cases for both bug identification and fix validation. Writing test cases is tedious; running them can be time-consuming; and (the most significant limitation) validating them through tests does not guarantee their correctness (Dijkstra again). Proof2Fix,19 based on Proof2Test, implements a static APR approach.

The tool chain (Figure 4) is derived from the standard workflow in APR by replacing tests with proofs. The process starts with verifying a program using a prover (here, AutoProof). If the prover detects a fault, Proof2Test generates counterexamples, each of which represents a failing execution trace, in which the program goes to a state that violates a desired property. Traditional APR techniques analyze failing tests (usually generated manually) to identify any common elements that might pinpoint the cause of the failure; Proof2Fix uses the same idea but with tests replaced by counterexamples generated automatically and statically.

The generation of abstract general properties from counterexamples uses Daikon,13 an inference tool that produces a set of counterexample invariants: predicates on the input variables that hold in the counterexamples, matched to a set of patterns (equality between variables or with constants, linear relations e1 = a · e2 + b or e1 = a · old e2 + b, etc.) The invariants make it possible to produce candidate fixes for either the contract or the implementation. (Empirical studies30 indicate that bugs arise from both kinds of mistake.) AutoProof then filters out invalid fixes, retaining only the fixes that pass the proof (they remove the original proof failure and introduce no new one). Valid choices can then be presented to the programmer. Neither at the bug-finding nor the bug-fixing stage is there any need to invent test data or to produce a test harness.

Evaluation of fixing 80 proof failures shows19 that the approach can produce meaningful, formally validated fixes. It generates at least one valid fix for 82.5% of all failures and at least one programmer-approved fix for 37.5% of them. A fixing session takes about one minute. Proof2Fix is most effective for failures caused by two types of faults: incorrect source expression in an assignment and incorrect condition in a conditional instruction. In both cases, the inferred counterexample invariants correctly characterize the faulty cases that need to be ruled out. However, the approach is not good at fixing failures caused by too-weak contracts, as the generated counterexamples exhibit too much diversity.

Proofs as a Foundation for Efficient Test Suite Generation

When the verification results in multiple failures, Proof2Test produces a number of different tests. The seeding contradiction (SC)21 strategy takes advantage of this possibility.

Every serious software project needs a regression test suite, essential to managing the project’s evolution by ensuring that new developments do not invalidate previously working functionality. (Software engineering history includes numerous examples of regression bugs, such as the 2012 Knight Trading Group bug, which lost the firm $440 million in 45 minutes and almost bankrupted it, and the July 2024 CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor update.) Aside from the practical advice of including a test for every case that failed at some point in the project’s history, it is very difficult to produce a regression test suite with high coverage of all the possible execution paths.

At first sight, the Proof2Test techniques described earlier seem inapplicable, since they deal with faulty programs, whereas we need a regression test suite for a working program. The idea behind seeding contradiction is, as the name suggests, that we will make a correct program incorrect—in many different ways—by inserting (“seeding”) a bug in every branch. While counterintuitive at first (the usual goal in software engineering is to go from incorrect to correct!), this idea enables us to benefit from the preceding techniques, which generate counterexamples for faulty programs. Under suitable conditions, a counterexample for an incorrect program can be an example (a case of correct behavior) for the corresponding correct program.

Proof2Test, with SC, inserts a faulty instruction (“trap property”)14 into every control branch, shown in Figure 5. The instruction is a special case of the instruction check p end, which states that the Boolean property p must hold at the corresponding program point, causing the verification to fail if it cannot guarantee it. (Execution, if attempted, would cause an exception if p does not hold at run time.) With False for p, the branch will fail to verify and the Proof2Test mechanisms of the previous section will generate the corresponding counterexample. The technique actually works for an incorrect program as well as for a correct one. Even though it uses a prover normally intended for programs equipped with contract elements (preconditions, postconditions, class and loop invariants, loop variants), it is applicable to uncontracted programs, as shown in this example.

By construction, the generated test suite achieves 100% branch coverage for feasible branches (excluding unreachable ones, which no test can possibly exercise). Proof2Test goes beyond branch coverage in two complementary ways:

  • MC/DC: On option, Proof2Test enforces the “modified condition/decision coverage” criterion, recommended in several important industrial software safety standards and particularly observed in the aerospace industry.b

  • Loop unrolling: The body of a standard “while” or “until” loop, by definition, can be executed a variable number of times, but branch coverage only needs a path with zero execution and another with at least one execution. In other words, it treats a loop like a conditional, missing bugs that arise only with other numbers of execution. Proof2Test includes a loop unrolling mechanism, which considers loop bodies executed (“unrolled”) any number of times, up to a user-settable maximum determined in consideration of performance constraints.

Our measurements of the results of enforcing MC/DC and loop unrolling23 indicate that both enhancements uncover bugs that plain branch coverage misses. The example programs, though significant and in some cases sophisticated (coming, for example, from verification competitions), are still small, so we refrain from sweeping conclusions, but the results are encouraging:

  • MC/DC increases the number of found bugs by 12.2% over branch coverage, growing to 14.6% for programs with complex multiple-condition decisions.21 This result is significant, since there is a certain skepticism toward MC/DC in the testing community (due in part to the original papers’ lack of empirical results)—some authors even dismiss the approach.4

  • Loop unrolling uncovers more faults as the depth of unrolling increases. Measurements show an improvement of 14.5% over plain branch coverage with 5-level unrolling, uncovering 86.1% of all faults.23 The rise of detected faults is steep for small unrolling levels (≤ 5); going from 1 to 2 brings a 9% improvement. Beyond 5, the effect decreases (by 3%, from 5 to 8).

Many advanced test-generation techniques, such as directed automated random testing and concolic testing,36 still require some code execution. The techniques described here are entirely static: They perform verification, using a prover, but do not execute the program and hence do not require test data (although they generate such data) or test harnesses. As noted, they work on correct as well as incorrect programs. If a program calls a routine with a precondition, the generated tests will satisfy the preconditions thanks to SC’s constraint-solving techniques.

The results summarized above, from empirical studies,21–23 are achieved with reasonable performance. The SC strategy produces a test suite much faster than some of the dynamic techniques, such as IntelliTest,37 previously known as Pex, a symbolic execution test-generation tool for .NET, and AutoTest, a test-generation tool for Eiffel using adaptive random testing, specifically ARTOO.8 For a typical small program, SC requires approximately 0.5 seconds to generate a 100%-branch-coverage test suite; that is about 50 times faster than IntelliTest and 500 times faster than AutoTest. Adding MC/DC multiplies the generation time by about two and the test suite’s size (an important concern in practice since a good software process runs test suites frequently) by a factor of less than 10. Depending on the complexity of the loop’s control-flow structures, adding unrolling for test generation would lead to a different increase in generation time. For plain loops (with neither embedded conditionals nor nested loops), it will lead to a roughly linear growth in generation time as the unrolling depth increases. While for nested loops or loops with more complex conditionals embedded inside, as more failing instructions are introduced during test generation, the increase in generation time becomes more substantial. The evaluation in Huang et al.23 shows that for the programs with nested loops, the time increases exponentially and becomes unacceptably high (more than an hour) when the unrolling depth reaches 8.

Related Work

A number of previous or parallel efforts turn counterexamples, generated from failed verification, into diagnostic messages. The Boogie Verification Debugger (BVD)26 allows programmers to “debug” Boogie proof-failure reports statically.26 Other tools7,32 pursue similar goals. These approaches provide static traces for analysis; the approach reported here goes further by producing a dynamic trace and actual tests that programmers can run to see concretely what is going on.

Many testing projects have used SMT solving techniques to generate tests. Some, such as Klee,6 PathCrawler,40 Pex/IntelliTest,37 and CUTE,36 are based on symbolic execution. They explore paths in a program and use a constraint solver to reason about their feasibility. These strategies include a dynamic component, and as a result cannot provide guarantees of exhaustive branch coverage. The testing strategies reported in the present work are static.

The earliest work we know to have applied this idea1 generates tests for low-level C programs using bounded model checking (BMC),25 producing test suites with exhaustive branch coverage. A more recent variant, for Java bytecode, is JBMC,5 where each verification run activates only one assertion at a time, producing one counterexample (the C version1 uses compile-time macros, one for each block to avoid actually generating multiple programs). In contrast, the SC framework produces only one program, using a single runtime variable representing the block number. Similarly, Beyer et al.3 extend the software model checker Blast to generate test suites of full coverage with respect to given predicates. BMC-based approaches rely on the correctness of the bound of the execution trace: If the bound is not set correctly, some branches might not be covered, requiring more verification runs to obtain a better bound. The SC approach does not need such mechanisms. An approach34 that applies ideas of fault injection for generating tests (building on work on using counterexamples for program repair35) in Hoare-style verification exploits counterexamples produced by the OpenJML9 verification tool to generate unit tests in JUnit format. These approaches all bear similarities to the work discussed here, which seems to provide the most far-ranging and unifying collection of proof-test combination techniques, from exploiting proof failures to counterexample minimization, test generation covering several code-coverage measures, and automatic program repair.

Automated test generation is an active research area (e.g., Gorla et al.16) that in recent years has increasingly used LLMs, generally leading to average coverage levels between 75% and 90%. Proof2Test is much more efficient. LLMs can also serve to generate specifications automatically,27 though questions remain: While such specifications might make the code provable, they might also be the wrong specifications, preventing the generation of some relevant tests.

The present work distinguishes itself by the use of Eiffel. While it can be viewed as a limitation, this choice also provides a considerable advantage, since it does not require an addition to another language (as does JML for Java) but rather uses an existing (ISO-standardized) language, taking advantage of the built-in contract mechanism and hence directly using the original contract-equipped source code for both tests (with EiffelStudio’s mechanism for evaluating assertions during testing) and proofs. Users of other languages may view these results as those of “laboratory work,” using ideal conditions to pave the way for others to extend the results to different environments.

Conclusion

The work presented here suffers from a number of limitations. Examples so far are still small, although some involve sophisticated algorithms. Some (but not all) of the applications  assume that the programs have been equipped with contracts, a step that not all programmers are prepared to take. And the program-repair applications so far have mostly covered variables of basic types and need to be extended to complex data structures.

These results, however, are promising, in particular on the performance side: Verification is faster than running many tests, an advantage that grows rapidly with the program’s size and complexity. More generally, any arguments claiming programmers allegedly do not want to write contracts should be weighed against the tasks that programmers must carry out in today’s dominant test-based approach. The commonly used phrase automatic testing, in its current meaning, is a misnomer, obscuring the unpleasant reality: the enormous burden that test-case generation, still largely a manual task, imposes on programmers. (AI tools will help, but they will also help write contracts.) With a static approach, that task can be automated.

More generally, program proofs and dynamic tests pursue the same ultimate goal of software correctness. This article has shown that one can treat them as complementary rather than exclusive. We have seen three major applications of the idea, exploiting the features of SMT solvers underlying modern proof tools: turning failed proofs, often elusive to the programmer, into directly usable tests (especially after minimization) evidencing the failure, which brings examples to human scale; generating 100%-coverage test suites entirely automatically; and providing guaranteed bug fixes. Today’s tools are still imperfect but they point the way to a major leap forward in the effectiveness of software verification and repair, combining the best of what the software engineering community has learned from both tests and proofs.
