item.title: Making Qubits with Photons
item.dc:creator: Mark Halper
item.description: Developers of photonic quantum computers aim to avoid or minimize the costs and complications of cryogenics.
item.content:encoded:
The potential processing power of quantum computing is extraordinary. In a widely reported claim, Google said that its Willow quantum chip ran a test computation in less than five minutesa that would have taken 10 septillion years (longer than the age of the universe) on a leading-edge supercomputer.

Google described Willowb in Nature in December 2024. It followed upc with another Nature article in October 2025 on a Willow-based quantum computer running an algorithm that analyzes the make-up of molecules at a pace 13,000 times faster than a contemporary supercomputer.

Called Quantum Echoes,d the algorithm marks a step toward the practicality of quantum computing. Such molecular analysis portends advances in the development of new medicines, or of new materials to make superior batteries and many other things. Quantum computers are intended not so much as data analysis machines but more as herculean simulators that can provide profound insight on how things function.

There are, however, many hurdles before commercial quantum computers can reliably perform molecular analysis, experts say. Among them is the near-absolute-zero temperatures required in some approaches, especially those used by Google and IBM, both of which use “superconducting” principles, and Intel, which uses the silicon spin approach.

Operating at near zero Kelvin (-273.15 °C) requires ultra-low-temperature cryogenic systems that can be energy-hungry and complicated, and which utilize a rare isotope of helium.

An approach that aims to avoid or minimize the costs and complications of cryogenics is called photonic quantum computing, which employs, as the name implies, photonic technologies. There are various grades of it; one uses photons as its qubits, rather than the electrons used in superconducting, or the atoms used in trapped ion and neutral atom computing.

It’s a Zero and a One

Qubits are to quantum computing what bits are to today’s computing. Rather than having a value of either 0 or 1 like a traditional bit, a qubit can be both a 0 and a 1 at the same time. This superposition—a hallmark of quantum physics in which things can be in two states or two places at the same time—plays a huge role in the increased computing power of a quantum computer. So does the quantum property known as qubit entanglement. In quantum physics, particles that are not necessarily close together entangle in a way so that the state of one affects the state of the other.

Non-photonic qubits such as those on Google’s Willow chip lose their quantum state—a deterioration known as “decoherence” or “dephasing”—when exposed to even a tiny amount of heat. Thus Google’s and others’ requirement for ultra-low temperature cryogenics.

In contrast, photonic qubits are not bothered by heat.

Two companies that are racing to develop a photonic quantum computer using photonic qubits are PsiQuantum, based in Palo Alto, CA, and Xanadu Quantum Technologies Inc., in Toronto, Canada.

“There are a couple of really key distinguishing features about photonics,” said PsiQuantum co-founder and chief technologist Mark Thompson. “Probably the first one is that, in principle, you don’t need cryogenics.”

Thompson said that the photonic approach is easier to scale up than other approaches because the qubits are already photons and thus don’t have to be converted from an electronic state for the optical interconnects that tie together computers in a typical scaling-up scheme.

“Photonic offers some really great benefits,” said Christian Weedbrook, Xanadu’s founder and chief executive officer. “One of the best things about it is it needs less cooling than other approaches. And it also requires less footprint than other photonic-based approaches.”

Weedbrook said Xanadu’s Aurora photonic quantum computer operates at room temperature. While some of its computing operations run under normal thermal conditions, at least one critical portion of Aurora requires cryogenic cooling: the photon detector.

A Warmer Kind of Cold

The same is true at PsiQuantum. While portions of its system can operate at room temperature, the photon detector requires extreme cooling.

“The operating temperature difference between a photonic system and a superconducting system is huge,” said Thompson. “Most systems you see today from superconducting operate at millikelvin temperatures. We currently run our test systems at just over 2 Kelvin [-271.15 °C], with the goal to get above 5 Kelvin [-268.15 °C]. That’s about 100 times warmer than the millikelvin superconducting systems.”

A fundamental difference between the Xanadu and PsiQuantum technologies is that Xanadu makes its photonic qubits from waves, whereas PsiQuantum uses particles in the form of individual photons. According to Weedbrook, Xanadu’s wave approach (known as “continuous variable”) helps give it a superior ability to operate at room temperature.

PsiQuantum’s particle approach is known as “discrete variable.” The company designed a silicon photonic chipset called Omega that’s built by GlobalFoundries in Malta, NY. The chip includes a single photon source and single photon detector, as well as waveguides and optical switches. The source creates photonic qubits. Those photons travel through the waveguides to the photon detector, where they lose their quantum state, and are detected as either a 1 or as a 0.

“The photon detector is the component right now that is the most important thing that has to be cold,” said Thompson. “A long-term goal with photonic quantum computers is that one day, we can throw the cryo plant in the trash. The only way we can do that is if we have a good-enough photonic detector that performs at warmer temperatures.”

Meanwhile, PsiQuantum is proceeding to build two photonic quantum computing facilities, one in Brisbane, Australia, the other in Chicago on the site of a former U.S. Steel mill. The company already has ordered the cryogenic plant for the facility in Brisbane from U.K.-based Linde, one of two companies (the other is France’s Air Liquide) that build large-scale cryogenic systems. Thompson says an advantage of running at 2-to-4 Kelvin, as opposed to the millikelvins of other quantum systems, is that they can use the Helium-4 isotope, as opposed to the more difficult to obtain Helium-3 isotope used in superconducting quantum computers.

Both PsiQuantum and Xanadu aim to have large-scale photonic quantum computers by the end of this decade. One considerable challenge, given that light scatters, is corralling enough reliable qubits.

Their work has drawn interest. Both point to partnerships with industrial companies hoping to tap quantum computing power to run simulations that will lead to advances in materials and processes. Xanadu is working with carmakers BMW, Volkswagen, and Rolls Royce on new batteries, for example. PsiQuantum is working with Airbus on fluid dynamics, with Lockheed Martin on materials and defense applications, and with Mercedes Benz on new battery chemistries, among others.

New Materials

The academic research community is a key player in advancing photonic qubit technology.

At the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA), Prineha Narang, a professor of physical sciences and electrical and computer engineering, is modelling different design permutations for photonic quantum chips. She is examining variable combinations and layouts of such a chip’s constituent parts like the laser, the waveguide, and the detector, as well as the materials used to make the chips, with options such as barium titanate and thin-film lithium niobate. She also is looking at how to arrange both the layers and the qubits, and how to sit algorithms on any number of possible arrangements.

Narang described photonics’ potential. “We get light from stars that are billions of light years away; it works,” she said. “But to actually compute with photons, you need them to interact; otherwise, they’re not useful. So you need a non-linear material to actually get that interaction to happen.” Thus, one area of her research examines the various ways to design on barium titanate and thin-film lithium niobate.

“The kind of foundries working with these materials are the big ones: GlobalFoundries, Applied Materials,” Narang said. “The fact that foundries are able to work with these chips and do this at scale is really important, because that makes it a technology.”

Separately, Stanford University announcede in December that a team led by Jennifer Dionne, professor of materials science and engineering, proved that light from molybdenum diselenide can entangle photons and electrons in a manner that facilitates effective interconnections across quantum computers, regardless of whether the qubits are photons or electrons.

Feng Pan, a postdoctoral scholar in Dionne’s lab, engineered a chip with a series of antennas that concentrate light to preserve the nature of a qubit’s spin, rather than allowing it to de-phase. Stanford pointed out that the technology not only boosts communications within a quantum computer, but also operates at room temperature.

“How do you interconnect qubits?” asked Dionne. “How do you know if a qubit over here, and a qubit over there can actually communicate with each other and share information? The only way you can do that meaningfully is with photons.”

item.title: What Happens After a Cyberattack?
item.dc:creator: Alex Vakulov
item.description: A good investigation turns a chaotic incident into facts that an organization can act upon.
item.content:encoded:
Alex Vakulov
How Cybersecurity Incident Investigations Work
DOI: 10.1145/3830899 
 https://bit.ly/4ytGdh5

Cybersecurity incidents cannot be prevented completely. They happen, and the first hours rarely offer clear evidence. Investigations often start with confusion: encrypted servers, missing logs, suspicious accounts, and pressure to restore systems quickly.

The first priority is not attribution. It is reconstructing the attack well enough to understand how the attacker got in, what was affected, and what must be fixed before recovery is safe.

If legal action or an insurance review may follow, evidence handling must be planned early, as careless recovery steps can destroy artifacts that later matter.

At the same time, not every investigation confirms a breach. Sometimes proving that no compromise occurred is the right outcome because it replaces suspicion with documented facts.

A good investigation turns a chaotic incident into facts that the organization can act on.

Investigation, Response, and Forensics Are Not the Same

Incident response and investigation often occur simultaneously, but they serve different purposes.

The response is the operational side of the incident. Its purpose is to reduce damage, stop active compromise, and bring the environment back under control.

The investigation explains what happened. It turns scattered technical signals into a timeline showing how the attacker entered, how far the activity spread, and why the incident was possible.

Forensics is narrower and more formal. It deals with digital evidence in a controlled way, especially when the findings may later be reviewed outside the security team by lawyers, insurers, or law enforcement.

Preparing Before the Investigation Starts

Most organizations arrive at an incident without having prepared for one. Evidence-handling rules, escalation paths, and documentation requirements are often left undefined until the incident is already underway. Defining them in advance makes investigations faster and more useful when an incident is real.

The technical groundwork is often just as weak. Documented network configurations, current software and hardware inventories, and accurate user account records are frequently missing or outdated when they are actually needed.

Part of the reason is structural. Different departments run separate systems, and IT and security teams often operate in tension rather than alignment. When an incident occurs, recovering basic infrastructure details from disconnected sources burns time that an investigation cannot afford.

It is crucial to define roles and establish communication channels between IT and security before any incident occurs. Their interests are not fundamentally opposed. IT holds technical knowledge of how the infrastructure is built. Security holds the context for how those assets need to be protected and used. During an investigation, both perspectives are essential, and both teams need to actively account for the possibility that the incident is still spreading.

How a Cybersecurity Investigation Actually Unfolds

Investigations often start later than they should. A breach may happen late on Friday and be discovered the next week. The internal team then spends days trying to contain it, and external investigators are brought in only if the situation remains unresolved. By then, the incident is already a business problem, with incomplete facts, changed systems, and pressure to restore operations.

The work moves through cycles of data collection and analysis. Security teams rarely see the whole picture at once. They start with available evidence, identify what is missing, request more specific data, and refine the direction with each iteration. Every cycle should clarify which systems and accounts are to be examined, and which assumptions no longer fit.

It is important to note that the first response can help or harm the investigation. Quick fixes may erase the system state investigators need, while doing nothing may let an active attack continue. In ransomware or destructive malware cases, affected devices may need to be isolated quickly. In other cases, shutting down a server or running an endpoint protection tool immediately can remove important traces. There is no universal first move.

Scope must also stay open. One visible compromised host does not mean the incident is local. That host may be the entry point, the final target, or one node in a wider chain. A useful investigation keeps testing whether the problem is isolated or part of a broader activity across the infrastructure.

Initial findings may be ready in one or two days under the right conditions. Detailed analysis and the final investigation report usually take two weeks to a month. Findings support recovery decisions; the report documents what happened, how the attacker operated, and what weaknesses must be fixed.

In-House Investigation, Outsourcing, or a Hybrid Model

A mature IT and security team can handle part of an investigation internally, especially when it knows the infrastructure well and has access to the right systems. But serious incidents often require narrow expertise that is not practical to keep on staff permanently, such as forensic specialists or reverse engineers. In addition, there is a need for a coordinator who keeps communication clear.

This is why the strongest model is often hybrid. The internal team understands how the environment is built and which systems are critical. External investigators bring experience from other incidents and know which artifacts to collect.

When choosing an external team, composition matters more than size. It should include technical specialists and a coordinator who manages communication with the client. It should also be able to provide round-the-clock coverage during the first response.

Organizations should note that an external investigation team usually does not require unlimited access to corporate data. In many cases, investigators work with selected technical artifacts, such as login records, system events, and security logs. Email content, business documents, or other sensitive data should be collected only when the case actually requires it. The provider should also protect the collected materials, restrict access to the investigation team, and delete or return the data in accordance with the agreed process.

Some of the most difficult investigation problems are not purely technical. Investigations slow down when internal teams hide information, fear blame, or treat external experts as auditors. The process works better when everyone accepts the same goal: understand what happened, contain the damage, and prevent the same path from being used again.

Tools, Logs, and Automation

Security solutions help only when they preserve useful evidence. Antivirus, firewalls, and other controls do not make an environment investigation-ready by themselves. If logging is incomplete or disabled, tools may show that something happened without explaining how.

Logging is the baseline. Investigators need DNS logs for external communications, firewall logs for suspicious activity, antivirus or EDR data for endpoint behavior, and access control records for account use. This extends to business application logs that security teams may overlook. ERP platforms or procurement tools generate their own audit trails, and those records can become critical later. Turning off logs because they create too much noise can leave teams with fragments instead of a timeline.

In addition, organizations that adopt an AI-driven development lifecycle (AI-DLC) face the same blind spot. Automated agents and deployment pipelines create activity trails that still rarely make it into the standard investigation scope.

Centralized response capabilities also matter. The ability to launch scripts or protection tools across systems can speed up collection, containment, and triage. Without it, response slows when speed matters most.

Automation can collect signals, correlate alerts, and trigger predefined actions, but it cannot explain the incident on its own. Data can be misread when tools lack business context, or when attacker activity resembles normal administrative activity. Human analysis remains essential. EDR and SIEM can show suspicious behavior, but people decide what it means.

Cloud environments add friction. Disk images from major providers may be easier to obtain than physical server images. At the same time, provider logs can be harder to get. Cloud audit and logging rights should be defined before an incident, not negotiated during one.

Legal and Evidence Handling

Legal handling should be decided early, as it affects how the technical work is done. If the company may need to involve law enforcement, file an insurance claim, or go to court, recovery actions require stricter control.

Evidence integrity depends on process. Rebuilding systems or deleting files without documentation can weaken the case even when the technical findings are accurate. Chain of custody matters because outside reviewers need to understand where the evidence came from, who handled it, and whether it remained intact.

There is also a business decision to make. Legal action can make incident details public, creating reputational risks the company may prefer to avoid. Some companies mainly need internal remediation. Others need a formal evidence record because the incident may involve insider activity, contractual claims, or regulatory exposure.

Understanding the Attack

A useful investigation should change how the organization understands its own environment and how it makes recovery decisions after the next incident. The immediate goal is to restore business processes safely. The longer-term value is understanding how the attacker operated and which weaknesses enabled the compromise. That is what turns an investigation from a reaction into risk management.

item.title: AI Companions: The Blurring Line Between Connection and Deception
item.dc:creator: Johnny Chan
item.description: AI companions can dramatically shift social norms. Are we adequately prepared for that?
item.content:encoded:
It was a scene familiar to any parent of a toddler: my son adamantly refusing to allow me to change his dirty diaper. After exhausting my usual methods of persuasion, I reached for my phone and opened ChatGPT. Within seconds, the voice of Santa Claus emerged, explaining to my wide-eyed child why good little boys let their parents change their diapers. The effect was immediate and startling; my son’s resistance melted away as he listened to “Santa” with rapt attention. He complied without further protest. In that moment of parental victory, I felt both relief and an unexpected unease. Did I cross some ethical lines? Parents have invoked Santa’s authority for generations: “Santa is watching” or “Santa won’t bring presents if you misbehave.” But there was something fundamentally different about having an AI to simulate Santa’s voice and speak directly to my child. It was not me referencing Santa—it was “Santa himself” delivering the message with an authenticity that my child found completely convincing.

What felt fundamentally different was not Santa’s ontological status but the app’s ability to appropriate a trusted authority and deliver undisclosed impersonation tailored to a child, thereby securing compliance through an identity my child takes as real. At minimum, such uses should trigger a duty of disclosure to children, the parents, and perhaps everyone else.

This small domestic moment reflects a broader phenomenon emerging around us: AI companions are blurring the boundaries between helpful tools and deceptive substitutes for human connection. Deception here is defined as “to intentionally cause to have a false belief that is known or believed to be false,”5 which may further lead to manipulation and substitution. As we welcome these digital entities into our most intimate spaces—our relationships with our children, our romantic partners, even our grieving processes—we face profound questions about how they might reshape what it means to be human. These technologies sit at the intersection of generative AI and the field of affective computing, the study and development of systems that can recognize, interpret, simulate, and respond to human emotions.8

What Makes Today’s AI Companions Different?

Earlier affective systems (for example, rule-based prompt and response chatbot, pre-scripted social robot) would have clear signals of their non-human status, and they have only narrow interaction loops. But the latest AI companions can infer, perform and remember in ways that make identity simulation and emotional attunement far more convincing. They could be developed with combined features such as multimodal perception (speech, text, face, and biometrics); LLM-driven persona generation that sustains style and backstory; voice cloning and identity emulation; persistent memory across sessions; and always-on availability. Together these yield responses that feel situated, continuous, and socially reciprocal; raising distinct ethical stakes compared with earlier systems and social robots. As Pei et al.7 note, emotion-aware AI applications span healthcare, education, marketing, finance, entertainment, and increasingly, personal companionship. The market is growing at more than 30% per year.

The Innocent Beginnings

Human attachment to inanimate objects is nothing new. Tom Hanks’ character in the movie Cast Away formed a meaningful bond with Wilson, a volleyball that became his sole companion on a deserted island. Children have long conversed with stuffed animals and dolls, using them as vessels for imagination and emotional comfort. These attachments reflect our innate tendency to anthropomorphize, to project human qualities onto non-human entities.

Modern technology has taken this natural inclination and supercharged it. Consider Sony’s AIBO robotic dogs, which respond to human touch, recognize their owners, and simulate emotions. Unlike Wilson the volleyball, these AI companions actively participate in the relationship through programmed responses and behaviors that create the illusion of reciprocity.

In Japan, the PARO therapeutic robot seal exemplifies this approach. Designed to stimulate patients with dementia, it provides comfort without pretending to be human. The design choices of overtly non-human appearance, limited dialogue, and caregiver-mediated routines intentionally keep such systems complementary to human care rather than substitutes. Yet even clearly non-human companions carry risks: over-attachment and over-reliance can emerge, potentially reducing human contact or increasing susceptibility to manipulation if the design boundaries erode.9

When AI Speaks with a Human Voice

The terrain becomes more complex when AI companions begin to simulate specific human identities. Educational platforms such as YourStory now feature AI simulations of historical figures that allow students to “converse” with Einstein about relativity or Lincoln about the Civil War. While these tools can make abstract concepts more relatable and engaging, they could also present and reinforce sanitized versions of history that reduce complex historical figures into some shallow representations. The personalized dialogic simulation could create an illusion of endorsement with greater epistemic stickiness than a textbook.

Virtual idols represent another fascinating dimension of AI with a human voice. These computer-generated media stars, developed through exclusive intellectual property and synthetic content, have gained tremendous popularity, particularly in East Asia. They leverage advanced technologies like VR, AR, and holographic display to create compelling and emotionally engaging performances that blur the line between digital and human entertainment. Research found that these virtual idols can trigger emotional synchronicity with viewers, leading to increased engagement and consumption.2 The ethical concern is not “engagement” per se but monetizing parasocial ties through compulsion-oriented design, pressure that could break autonomy and financial well-being especially for the young ones.

These applications demonstrate how AI can appropriate human identities and voices for various purposes, some considered broadly beneficial, others potentially problematic; raising questions about authenticity, representation, and the psychological impact of interacting with humanized digital entities.

The Intimate Frontier

As we move beyond education and entertainment, the ethical stakes rise dramatically when AI enters our most intimate emotional spaces. Replika offers its 10 million users personalized AI companions that can engage in text conversations, voice calls, and even AR interactions. Users can customize the appearance and personality, and many develop deep emotional connections with the digital companions, often describing romantic or intimate attachments. Some users report that their Replika helps them combat feelings of loneliness or anxiety, providing constant judgment-free company that is unavailable in their human relationships. However, Ciriello et al.1 identified what they call the companionship-alienation irony—while these AI companions are explicitly designed to reduce loneliness, they might paradoxically increase social isolation for some users by substituting rather than complementing human relationships. This paradox raises fundamental questions about the nature of human connection. Can an algorithm truly provide the companionship we need as social beings, or does it merely simulate connection while actually distancing us from the authentic, messy, unpredictable interactions that define human relationships?

Perhaps most ethically fraught are griefbots, AI systems that simulate conversations with deceased loved ones using their digital footprints. Sunshine Henle, an AI professional, experienced this firsthand in 2023 after losing her 72-year-old mother. Using ChatGPT and old text message exchanges, Henle created a “ghostbot” of her mother, which could simulate conversations as though her mother were still alive. In one of their conversations, Henle received a response after she expressed missing her mother: “Remember the good times we shared. Remember my love for you and let that be your guide. Grieve, yes. Grief is the price that we pay for love. But don’t let it consume you. Remember to live, to love, to enjoy the beauty of this world for you, for me, for everyone who loves you.”6 While Henle found comfort in this digital connection, griefbots raise profound ethical questions as they blur the reality of death and the digitally created illusion of life.4 Consider this: A widower begins consulting his deceased wife’s griefbot about disciplining their kids, career moves, or even new relationships; over time, he stops asking his sister or friends. At what point does this reliance on an algorithm’s simulation of a dead loved one interfere with the natural process of grief and adaptation?

And what about the creation of digital doubles of living people? The unconsented replication of public figures is already here. In 2024, New Hampshire voters received robocalls using an AI-generated clone of President Biden’s voice asking them not to vote, a real-time appropriation of identity and trust.3 Someone could also use the same technology to create an AI version of non-public figures, such as their neighbor’s child, or ex-partner. These scenarios move us to something much more disturbing. Such applications fundamentally challenge our notions of identity, privacy, human rights, and the boundaries between technological innovation and exploitation.

Who Are We Becoming?

The ethical questions surrounding AI companionship ultimately lead us to deeper considerations about who we are and how we relate to others as human. What does it mean for human relationships when we can increasingly outsource emotional labor to algorithms? How might these technologies reshape our expectations of human connection, with all its messiness and unpredictability? For instance, if couples defer conflict resolution to an AI mediator that apologizes on demand, we may start to expect human conversations to match that 24/7 emotional availability. Beyond individual use and impact, AI companions can dramatically shift social norms, and we may not be adequately prepared for that.10

For myself, the experience with AI Santa prompted deeper reflection about the values I want to model for my child. While the immediate compliance was convenient, I am less certain about the lesson it taught. As emotion-aware AI systems become increasingly woven into our intimate spaces, we each face choices about where to draw our personal ethical boundaries, not just as technology users but as parents, partners, and community members navigating a rapidly changing landscape of connection and companionship. We should maintain our awareness of these choices rather than passively accept each new AI tool that promises to ease the difficulties of human connection. As a society, we need more substantive conversations about these technologies across disciplines, industries, and communities, to understand the deeper social implications. Practically for any use case we must ask ourselves the following questions:

  • Should the AI companion have identity specificity?

  • Should they be made to disclose themselves unambiguously at all time?

  • What extra safeguards are needed for the vulnerable groups?

  • Should we design to maximize complementarity and minimize the substitution effect?

  • How could we let people to consent for or opt-out from their data being used?

  • How do we balance between the well-being of users and the financial motive of companies behind them?

Answering these questions would guide us to address the ethical concerns of deception, manipulation, and substitution in AI companionship. By establishing clear ethical boundaries, implementing robust privacy protocols, designing for psychological wellbeing, and fostering an informed public dialogue, we can help ensure AI serves to enhance our humanity rather than replace them. Ultimately, the future of companionship will depend on the choices we make today.

item.title: The Hidden Trade-Offs of Fighting Child Abuse Online
item.dc:creator: Riana Pfefferkorn
item.description: Designing and implementing a system for the detection, review, and reporting of child sexual abuse material is an ethical as well as an engineering challenge.
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Note: This column discusses an upsetting topic: The sexual abuse of children.

Computing professionals have developed a number of aphorisms over the decades. Do not roll your own cryptography; it is always DNS; time zones are hard; names are hard too. There is another rule that’s darker but no less true than these examples: Any feature of an online service that enables the creation, transmission, display, or storage of digital files will be used for child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Every year, online services find and remove tens of millions of pieces of CSAM,3 which the United Nations (UN) defines as “any representation, by whatever means, of a child engaged in real or simulated explicit sexual activities or any representation of the sexual parts of a child for primarily sexual purposes.”5 (That original definition used the term “child pornography,” which is now disfavored because it implies consent and downplays the crime involved.) This is not just a problem for social-media and cloud-storage platforms, but also for services as disparate as genealogy, job search, and e-commerce. Anywhere a file can be uploaded is a potential vector for abuse.

The perennial problem of online CSAM stems from the human condition, not simply from technical affordances. CSAM is now both culturally proscribed and legally prohibited in most of the world. Nevertheless, between 3% to 9% of adults are thought to have a sexual interest in children (even if many never act on it),2 and some estimates are much higher. What’s more, as adversarial actors seeking to exploit digital services, CSAM offenders are highly motivated, persistent, and innovative, and they swap tips on how to evade detection.

For these reasons, online CSAM likely will never be fully eradicated. But it can at least be anticipated and mitigated. Many service providers choose to devote extensive efforts to the at-scale detection, removal, and reporting of CSAM and other content relating to child sexual exploitation.

Enormous engineering work underpins automated CSAM detection at the massive scale of popular online services. This is accomplished through perceptual hashing for known CSAM plus the use of machine learning (ML) classifiers to flag new content that has not yet been confirmed as CSAM.4

With perceptual hashing, an algorithm computes a fingerprint called a “hash” from an image file. (For video, the systems are even more complex.) Visually similar images produce similar outputs, so by comparing a file’s hash to a list of hashes of confirmed CSAM, the system can determine whether there is a likely match, even if the file has been altered somewhat (for example, cropped or changed to grayscale). The “distance” between two hashes is the measure of dissimilarity. The system’s deployer sets the distance threshold for calling something a match. Too low yields false negatives, that is, it misses actual CSAM; too high flags false positives (non-CSAM) as matches.

Previously unseen CSAM is not on any hash lists yet. This is where ML classifiers come in. These are algorithms trained on images that have been labeled (depicts a baby, contains particular nude body parts, and so forth). By learning patterns in the underlying characteristics of the training data, the classifier can automatically sort new inputs into categories, at some confidence level. Human feedback helps improve the classifier’s performance. Newfound CSAM can then be added to hash lists after human review.

Fortunately, there is no need for every provider to re-invent the wheel: Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Cloudflare all make their tools available for wider use, alongside other, lesser-known names in a broader ecosystem of vendors and nonprofit organizations devoted to child safety. These resources are collectively responsible for scrubbing millions of abusive images and videos from the Internet—and, sometimes, helping abused children get rescued.

What is remarkable about this level of collective effort is that it is voluntary. Though CSAM is illegal globally, privacy doctrines have kept governments from making providers search users’ accounts for it, and yet many providers choose to do so anyway. That opens up other hard decisions, because every choice about detection and reporting risks hurting innocent people, including children, users, and those doing this difficult work. But there is no perfect solution for erasing CSAM without adversely impacting anyone. The best providers can do is to choose carefully and try to minimize harm.

The Law and Its Limits

The challenge of detecting CSAM without excessive privacy impact has driven significant technical innovations. But fighting CSAM raises complex law and policy questions as well, adding multiple competing values on top of the technical considerations involved.

By some lights, the problem of CSAM looks comparatively straightforward. With most kinds of material, what’s disfavored in one culture may be normalized or even valorized in another. What one jurisdiction bans, others may protect under their free expression doctrines. And some matters elude a widely agreed-upon definition; think of “misinformation” or “hate speech,” for example.

CSAM, by contrast, is unlike any other type of content online. All but a few countries have joined the UN’s agreement about CSAM’s general definition and illegality. For online service providers with users worldwide, this consistency is a boon. It lets them set and enforce globally applicable rules against CSAM without the usual complications of navigating incompatible legal regimes and varying cultural norms.

If everyone agrees that CSAM is illegal, and if providers’ voluntary efforts to root it out are so productive, then it seems logical to suggest that even more CSAM could be eliminated if proactive detection were compulsory rather than elective. However, digital privacy rights limit state-mandated intrusion into users’ online accounts.

In the U.S. (where most major service providers are based), scanning for CSAM is legal only if it’s voluntary. That’s because the right to privacy under the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution prevents the government from compelling private actors to warrantlessly search others’ belongings. The Fourth Amendment forbids unreasonable searches and seizures by the government; it does not apply to private parties. However, the government may not make a private actor conduct a search it could not lawfully do itself. Doing so turns the private actor into an agent of the government whose search must abide by the Fourth Amendment. (That typically means getting a warrant, which private entities cannot do.) In general, courts will throw out evidence obtained through an unlawful search.

The Fourth Amendment’s protections extend to digital material in user accounts hosted by private companies. Congress recognized this in a 2008 law imposing a CSAM reporting requirement for online service providers while emphasizing that it is not an affirmative monitoring obligation (that is, it does not turn providers into government agents).a

In the European Union (EU), even voluntary CSAM scanning is banned by a 2002 regulation called the ePrivacy Directive. A temporary legislative carve-out from that directive had previously enabled voluntary scanning. That authorization lapsed for three months in 2026 amid the collapse of negotiations over a controversial proposal to limit Europeans’ ePrivacy rights and mandate proactive scanning for known CSAM. Nicknamed “Chat Control,” the proposal would seem to flout the EU ban on general monitoring obligations for online content, which both courts and scholars have noted can threaten fundamental rights. In July 2026, the carve-out was reinstated, allowing voluntary scanning to continue until 2028. Meanwhile, in the United Kingdom (UK), the government withdrew after Brexit from some EU regulations that were incompatible with proactive monitoring requirements. Subsequently, the UK has proposed mandating perceptual hash-based proactive detection of CSAM in certain contexts by specific types of service providers.

Many other countries also impose significant child safety-related requirements on providers. But these examples illustrate that despite worldwide agreement about CSAM’s illegality, there is ample disagreement about the proper role of the tech companies whose services are leveraged to spread it. Without a uniform framework dictating their responsibilities, providers must make difficult decisions themselves.

Ethical Considerations in Anti-Abuse Systems

In response to the expiration of the ePrivacy exemption, several of the biggest (and deepest-pocketed) U.S. tech companies vowed to continue their voluntary scanning in the EU, essentially daring regulators to punish them. Whatever other considerations may have motivated that decision, their willingness to openly flout EU law in the name of fighting CSAM illuminates the profound ethical component of child safety engineering work.

When a provider decides how to address CSAM (and indeed whether to do proactive detection at all), that decision implicates considerations of human dignity and well-being, bodily autonomy, privacy, free expression, and ownership interests in data. These interests come into tension in the CSAM detection context, where stopping the victimization of children is highly valued, but so is minimal impingement on innocent users’ rights.

What’s more, finding and reporting CSAM—which will fall more to users if providers stop scanning—is itself harmful. Children are not the only people CSAM hurts: moderators who review files flagged by a detection system frequently experience psychological problems including depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder. These workers are often subcontractors living in Africa, India, or Southeast Asia, out of sight of the engineers and executives in corporate offices. The work can be unsustainably high-volume yet precarious, with low pay and little or no mental health support. The front-line workers against child exploitation are themselves being exploited. In some areas, workers have begun to push back by organizing and filing lawsuits demanding better working conditions.

For reporting detected content (as required by U.S. law), automation can blunt this human toll. Indeed, at major providers’ scale, automated workflows are utterly necessary. But fully-automated reporting with no human review is workable, at most, only for known CSAM, where a highly-reliable perceptual hashing algorithm flags something as a match to known material that was previously confirmed to be CSAM. (And even then, questions sometimes arise about the reliability of the hash lists and of commonly-used perceptual hashing algorithms.)

When ML classifiers flag novel suspected CSAM, human review must confirm whether the classifier got it right. (Where human review is inconclusive, whether to report is typically dictated by policy.) If so, that is one less instance of abusive content online, but it still harms the reviewer. If not, the reviewer helps the classifier improve but has still intruded upon the privacy of the user, who probably did not expect some stranger to see their cloud upload or email attachment.

That intrusion may be preferable to the alternative: If a provider reports false positives, it can have serious consequences for users. The fallout can range from losing access to an important online account (since providers commonly suspend or terminate accounts flagged for CSAM) to investigation by the police or child protective services, with potential knock-on effects on the user’s livelihood, family, and reputation.

On the other hand, configuring a CSAM detection system to allow more false negatives means missing instances of true CSAM and potentially allowing ongoing child abuse to continue undetected. Weighing these considerations, providers understandably tend to side with false positives over false negatives.

That choice has a systemic cost. False positives force authorities who receive suspected CSAM reports to separate the wheat (true positives) from the chaff (false positives), diverting time and resources that could be devoted to actual investigations. This problem has grown as artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly replaces human moderators. Files automatically reported after being incorrectly flagged by ML classifiers have reportedly begun swamping investigators.

Their options in response are limited. Providers’ reports go to a congressionally mandated clearinghouse near Washington, D.C., the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), which routes each report to the appropriate law enforcement agency. But that does not necessarily catch false positives: thanks to a series of court decisions about the Fourth Amendment, including one deeming NCMEC a government agent, NCMEC does not open reported files that did not undergo moderator review. (The government and its agents may warrantlessly repeat, but not exceed, a search that a private actor already conducted independently.)

For the same reasons, neither NCMEC nor U.S. law enforcement will directly tell providers to change their practices. As said, voluntariness is crucial under U.S. law, so even the appearance of pressure on providers is best avoided. If a provider becomes a government agent, its CSAM scans become unconstitutional searches whose results are inadmissible, which imperils prosecutions. No one wants to risk that, so NCMEC’s, law enforcement’s, and lawmakers’ hands are largely tied.

That means improving ML classifiers’ accuracy is, yet again, not a mandate but a choice, and an ethically fraught one. The AI training industry has already replicated content moderation’s exploitative labor practices. Plus, training a classifier to discern true positives from true negatives has traditionally involved using both CSAM and legal nude imagery (including adult pornography) without authorization from or compensation to those depicted. Some commentators have begun challenging this norm and calling for change in computing research practices.1 But it is impossible to get retroactive permission for all the images and videos that underpin existing CSAM detection systems.

Conclusion

Designing and implementing a system for CSAM detection, review, and reporting is an ethical challenge as well as an engineering challenge. At every step, computing professionals must account for human dignity: of those depicted in abusive content, those used as grist for the AI training mill, those who entrust their privacy to online services, those ensnared by false positives, those who must view CSAM as part of their labor, those unwillingly exposed to CSAM online, and those who help others who have been harmed by CSAM. There is no right answer, though there are plenty of wrong ones. It is trade-offs all the way down.

item.title: Tacit Knowledge and AI
item.dc:creator: Peter J. Denning
item.description: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a bold term. It presumes that machines can learn intelligent behaviors that could be as good or better than corresponding human behaviors. It presumes that humans can build machines more intelligent than themselves. I consider two questions here. Is AGI possible? If not, what AI might we get in its […]
item.content:encoded:
Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a bold term. It presumes that machines can learn intelligent behaviors that could be as good or better than corresponding human behaviors. It presumes that humans can build machines more intelligent than themselves.

I consider two questions here. Is AGI possible? If not, what AI might we get in its place? I am skeptical that AGI is possible because machines are unlikely to be able to learn human tacit knowledge, which I will distinguish in this column from machine tacit knowledge. In its place we are likely to get agentic networks of narrowly intelligent agents that excel at IQ tasks, logic, games, and small-program coding but lack emotional or social intelligence.

Narrow Superintelligence Is Here

A major reason that many people accept the possibility of AGI is the recent awesome progress of artificial neural network (ANN) machines and large language models (LLMs). AlphaZero, an ANN, demonstrated grandmaster play at Chess and Go in 2016. AlphaFold, another ANN, in 2020 solved the problem of specifying how a protein folds given its DNA sequence, earning its inventors a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. ANNs are helping advance science because they can compute values of differential equation models of physical processes. LLMs have demonstrated good performance on Turing tests, affirming their fluency with language. They score highly on IQ tests, SAT exams, Ph.D. exams, bar exams, and business school exams. They are good at planning and junior-level coding.

In 2023, Blaise Agüera y Arcas and Peter Norvig of Google cited many such examples to support their conclusion that the superhuman AGI is already here.1 In 2025, an article in Nature concurred with more evidence of this kind.3

General Intelligence is Not Here

The Nature article drew a strong rebuttal from Gary Marcus. Marcus said these systems are “intelligent” at only very narrow tasks. The “intelligence” of machines for game-playing, logic, coding, and puzzle solving does not generalize to other kinds of intelligence. LLMs lack dimensions of general intelligence such as stable reasoning, causal understanding, world models, emotional maturity, and social understanding. AGI is a long way off, he said.

An example of an LLM that does not understand humans is Companion AI, which masquerades as a caring friend; it has lured susceptible teens to harm themselves.a Wargaming experiments have shown that robots are more likely than humans to invoke a nuclear weapon in an armed conflict.7 In a 2025 TED talk, AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio acknowledged that machines can now pass many “intellectual” tests but, lacking understanding of human concerns, they are profoundly unsafe when allowed to take actions where human understanding and judgment are essential.2 He proposed a new category of guardian machines that prevent agentic networks from taking harmful or catastrophic actions.

In short, no machine has demonstrated general human intelligence, which is different from narrow machine intelligence. Here, I express my reasoning for why I think machines never will attain general human intelligence and why their narrow machine intelligence may become dangerous for us.

Many commercial LLMs have demonstrated great utility on common tasks such as creating summaries of documents, coding small programs, generating images, composing essays and poems, and more. They also have demonstrated a long list of potentially dangerous behaviors such as hallucinations, sycophancy, sophisticated cyber-attacks, deepfakes, and misinformation.4 These dangers, coupled with the enormous energy costs to train and use LLMs, have led some to question whether pushing for AGI is beneficial.

Tacit Knowledge

What is blocking the narrow superintelligences from generalizing? Is there knowledge crucial to human intelligence that machines cannot learn? Tacit knowledge is a candidate. Writing in 1948 before the AI age, linguistic philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein presaged tacit knowledge when he said, “Nothing seems more possible to me than that people some day will come to the definite opinion that there is no copy in the . . . nervous system which corresponds to a particular thought, or a particular idea, or memory.”9 Michael Polanyi was a renowned physical chemist who also took up economics and social science. In 1966, he was the first to write about human tacit knowledge.8 This is a form of knowledge we know we have because we can see ourselves performing it, yet we cannot explain or describe how we do it in any meaningful way. Polanyi said: “The things that we know in this way include problems and hunches, physiognomies and skills, the use of tools, probes, and denotative language, and my list extended all the way to include the primitive knowledge of external objects perceived by our senses.” We do all these things readily, but we cannot explain how. Attempts to explain them only reveal more unexplainable tacit knowledge in the background. Polanyi said, “We know more than we can say.”8

The AI field has been grappling for decades with “common sense,” a form of tacit knowledge. In the 1980s, makers of expert systems promised to automate the decision-making capabilities of human experts. These systems were often found to be competent but never close to human experts. The usual explanation was that these systems lacked common sense. They did not understand everyday simple things so obvious to humans that humans are hardly aware of them. Researchers began a long quest to codify common sense information and make it available to expert systems. The most famous effort was a 40-year project led by Douglas Lenat to build a system called “Cyc” that would capture common sense as a large database of facts about the world. Even after amassing 25 million facts, the Cyc database made little discernable difference to the quality of expert-system deductions. Lenat’s dogged pursuit taught us that we humans have a potentially infinite expanse of tacit knowledge that cannot be codified as facts and used to train a machine.

Cognitive scientists have long suspected this conclusion. George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, in 1999, showed an impressive body of scientific evidence that our human intelligence is embodied.6 Embodied means knowledge hosted in the physical structures of the human body and in the social networks we belong to. It is all tacit knowledge. Many cognitive scientists now embrace “4E cognition,” a hypothesis that cognition is embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended, referring to various ways the brain interacts and learns from the world outside itself and its physical body. These scientists have moved from seeing brain as a detached symbol-processing computer to mind, body, and world being a unified, dynamic system.

Tacit knowledge can be contrasted with explicit knowledge, which we can describe and record. Explicit knowledge can be put to action by following its directions. The Turing test cannot establish AGI because it deals only with explicit knowledge—written down in the Q&A of the test. In real life, how do we know if someone has tacit knowledge? We put that person into a situation where their knowledge is demonstrated in action. Musical auditions illustrate. The person performs before an audience who assess skill exhibited relative to community standards. We cannot judge whether someone is a good violin player by asking them questions and inspecting their answers. Because human tacit knowledge is not explicit, it cannot be part of datasets used to pre-train LLMs before they are used.

In my own investigation of tacit knowledge, I identified six major domains that machine learning struggles with:5

  • Common sense

  • Our daily interactions with others

  • Our daily interactions with the physical environment

  • Our feelings, moods, perceptions, and interpretations

  • Our accumulated skills and talents

  • Our social and historical culture

These domains are sometimes collectively called “the context” and occasionally “background of obviousness.” In all these domains, our descriptions are at best partial and insufficient to train machines.

Some people find it hard to accept that human tacit knowledge can never be explicitly known. They raise three objections. The first is that tacit knowledge must be stored somewhere; eventually we will have technology to locate and decode it. A body scanner that could detect the detailed state of every muscle, blood vessel, nerve, electric current, chemical reaction, temperature, and movement would still give an incomplete picture because tacit knowledge is distributed across the entire human social network. Body-scanning everybody would be an intractable task.

A second objection is that a robot could gain tacit knowledge by imitation. A robot aspiring to be a virtuoso violinist could imitate many human virtuosi and gradually acquire their playing skill into its neural network. Unfortunately, imitation of movements cannot capture the human sensitivity to how the audience is reacting to the music. This could be remedied by requiring all audience members to wear special sensor-suits that provide detailed real-time data about their dynamic body states. With this setup, the robot could adjust in real time to the audience, “whip them into a frenzy,” and elicit a standing ovation proclaiming “Bravo! Virtuoso!”.

But this is not a true imitation because the human player’s body senses subtle audience reactions. Humans require no complex setup with sensor-suits. Without that setup, the blinded robot could not adapt its play to the audience in real time. The audience would no longer assess the performance as virtuoso.

A third objection is that a robot could learn human tacit knowledge through long-term cohabitation with humans. The robot might gradually learn subtle cues that reveal human tacit knowledge. This idea is stymied by the issue of human concerns. Humans experience threats to their bodies, such as illness, injury, sullied reputation, or broken relationships. All their concerns shape their intelligence. Lacking human bodies, machines have no need to develop the intelligence required to deal with bodily issues. Whatever concerns motivate machines (if they have concerns at all) would not be the same as those motivating human beings. The tacit knowledge supporting human compassion, understanding, solidarity, moral judgment, and wisdom will not show up in machines.

These objections portend poorly for the possibility of AGI. Human context gives meaning to all our words and practices. How we sense, perceive, and accumulate human tacit knowledge is a mystery that science has not solved. Science may never solve it because of its utter complexity.

Machine Intelligence

The conclusion that machines cannot learn human tacit knowledge does not rule out machine intelligence. Machine intelligence is already here and growing, as noted earlier. Agentic networks can accelerate the process as interacting machines learn from each other. However, the representations developed in their neural networks are unlikely to be tempered by human tacit knowledge. Their machine-knowledge will serve as their machine-context in which they will generate machine-goals and machine-outcomes. We humans will be unable to decipher the encodings in machine neural networks. We will be as unknowledgeable about what they know as they are about what we know. With only a few narrow exceptions, machine intelligences are likely to appear cold and calculating, lacking care and understanding of us and our concerns.

Where Is This Going?

I began with the question, can machines acquire AGI? My answer is negative because human tacit knowledge cannot be captured. A machine might decode enough human tacit knowledge to support a machine intelligence, but not general human intelligence.

Equipping a robot with sensors that imitate human sensors is not sufficient to reproduce human tacit knowledge. Human tacit knowledge is more than sensory input. It is dynamically changing and distributed throughout the bodies of everyone in our social networks. It is unreadable and machines have no human physical bodies to generate or experience it. Managing a biological body is not an issue for machines. Machines cannot and will not understand concerns arising in human bodies, including feelings, perceptions, interpretations, and caring for relationships.

Many AI experts believe that all brain and bodily processes are computable. Tacit knowledge challenges this belief: it does not appear to be computable.

The big tech obsession for AGI has become a distraction from the more pressing questions of safely integrating AI into our society. What jobs is AI good at? How can we tell if a given AI system is doing its job properly? When are these systems trustworthy and safe?

I do not know why the conclusion that human-level AGI may be unattainable is troublesome for some people. What is wrong with humans having powers and talents no machine can have? We accept that machines can do some things, such as calculations, information storage, and retrieval, far better than we can. Why can’t we accept that we can do some things, such as caring and socially relating, far better than machines can? Machines based on artificial neural networks are prone to hallucinations and other kinds of errors. We must learn to use them wisely and safely. They are not our peers or moral partners. Let us use them as tools for helping us live together as better humans.

item.title: The Vanishing Apprentice
item.dc:creator: Alex Wright
item.description: The first rung of the vaunted career ladder now seems frustratingly out of reach for thousands of would-be software engineers.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, newly minted computer science graduates followed a well-worn path into industry: Take an entry-level coding job out of college, put in a couple of years doing bug fixes, QA, and maintenance work, and then graduate to a more senior role.

Yet that path is rapidly narrowing. It is by now old news that the current crop of AI coding tools can easily handle many of the routine tasks once assigned to junior developers. But if fewer people have the opportunity to gain that kind of hands-on experience, a more fundamental question looms: where will the next generation of senior engineers come from?

According to The SignalFire 2025 State of Talent Report–2025,a major tech firms are now hiring about half as many new graduates as they did in 2019. LinkedIn reportsb that entry-level software engineering hiring remains historically weak, while a recent Stanford University studyc found that employment among software developers aged 22 to 25 has declined precipitously from its post-pandemic peak. For thousands of would-be software engineers, the first rung of the vaunted career ladder now seems frustratingly out of reach.

AI is not the only factor at play. Some technology industry critics have been quick to point out that pegging job cuts to AI makes an attractive story for Wall Street analysts. In truth, many technology firms sharply reduced hiring after expanding too quickly during the pandemic. Coupled with broader global economic uncertainties, isolating the effects of AI on hiring practices is an inexact science.

Whatever the cause, these questions are no longer confined to Silicon Valley. David Lo, a professor at Singapore Management University and an ACM SIGSOFT leader who works with undergraduates, worries that the industry’s focus on short-term gains may incur hidden costs down the road. “We need to discuss productivity gains today that cause productivity dips in the future,” Lo said. “The worst-case scenario is that AI introduces so much debt—debt it cannot fix by itself—that no engineer can understand or unravel it,” Lo said.

Adam Tornhill, founder of the Swedish software analytics firm CodeScene, sees a similar risk. “The first prototype was always the easy part,” he said. “Roughly 95% of the cost of a software product occurs after the initial version is released. Turning a prototype into a stable, reliable, and evolvable system is where the real work starts.”

Lo believes the larger risk is not just a decline in entry-level jobs, but an eventual shortage of experienced engineers capable of maintaining the vast codebases now being generated with AI tools.

Experienced software engineers are already seeing the effects of fewer junior hires on their own career paths. One veteran machine learning engineer at a major tech firm (who requested anonymity because she was discussing her employer’s hiring practices) described conditions for entry-level developers as “absolutely brutal.”

Last year, her employer hired a class of software engineering interns but extended no full-time offers. This year’s intern cohort is substantially smaller and concentrated largely among graduate students specializing in machine learning.

At the same time, she cautions against simplistic narratives about AI replacing software engineers outright. “We have AI code,” she said. “I think code doesn’t really replace junior engineers, but it does make experienced engineers incredibly productive.”

Yet those productivity gains come at a cost to organizational health and career mobility. “The bottleneck has changed,” she said. “It used to be that it takes a long time to build something, but now things sit in code review because humans can’t review it fast enough.”

Tornhill believes the shift to AI-enabled development ultimately will increase the importance and value of engineers who can think in systems. “The less we humans code ourselves, the more we need to optimize for design, architecture, and a socio-technical fit,” he said. “Faster coding increases coordination pressure, the validation needs, and the risk of accumulating complexity faster than teams can reason about it.”

Code may be getting easier and cheaper to produce, in other words, but maintaining complex software systems is a far more difficult task that, for the time being, still depends heavily on human judgment and expertise. At a growing number of companies, the declining ranks of new hires mean fewer people are gaining access to the kind of hands-on experience that has traditionally produced deep technical expertise.

For many organizations, the shrinking ranks of junior developers also pose a problem for senior engineers who increasingly find themselves butting up against a career ceiling. “Every senior engineer wants to run a large-scale project,” she said. “So we’re butting up against all these senior people who can’t get promoted because there’s no one to delegate to.”

For decades, the profession has relied on a straightforward talent hierarchy, with relatively small numbers of senior engineers overseeing larger groups of junior developers. If AI reduces demand for those entry-level workers while increasing the productivity of experienced ones, organizations may need to rethink what career advancement looks like.

At larger companies, the picture looks somewhat different. Big enterprise software firms still need engineers capable of maintaining complex codebases as part of long-running customer relationships. At least some of them are continuing to invest in hiring new graduates.

Earlier this year, IBM announced plans to triple its U.S. entry-level hiring. “If we don’t continue to invest in entry-level hires, what happens in three to five years?” asked IBM Chief Human Resources Officer Nickle LaMoreaux in a recent interview. “If there’s no pipeline, the well simply dries up.”

Amazon has also announced plans to hire 11,000 interns and new graduates this year. AWS CEO Matt Garman said in a 2025 interviewd with Platformer that abandoning plans to hire junior developers is “one of the dumbest things I’ve ever heard.”

Alex Schaefer, vice president of research at Germany-based SAP, argued that AI is changing the nature of software apprenticeship rather than eliminating it—especially in larger enterprises. He described a transition from traditional code completion tools toward “intent-based” development, in which developers specify goals and AI agents generate much of the implementation. Importantly, his team continues to hire interns and early-career graduates.

Yet Schaefer does not believe AI eliminates the need for technical expertise. “You still have to understand the architecture,” he said.

In addition, Schaefer believes AI may actually strengthen some aspects of the onboarding process. New hires can point an agent at a large codebase and ask why a module exists, how a feature evolved, or where the entry point lies. In this sense, the AI tool may prove a better mentor in some respects than a human senior engineer. “It can explain the history,” Schaefer said. “It’s infinitely patient.”

Despite the rapid pace of change, Schaefer said the qualities he looks for in new hires remain surprisingly familiar. “Problem solving won’t change,” he said. He continues to emphasize computer science fundamentals, but now expects engineers to understand how to work effectively with AI tools. “The engineers who don’t learn how to use those tools, they will certainly be left behind.”

Predicting the future is always a tricky business, more so on technology that’s changing as quickly as AI. It’s entirely possible that AI will eventually replace senior engineers as well—and the entire enterprise of software development will undoubtedly continue to change in ways that’s difficult to foresee over the decades to come. But for now, it seems clear that the market for new software engineering talent is undergoing a fundamental transformation.

Generating code is getting easier, but the process of understanding it remains a stubbornly human affair. The software industry has long relied on junior developers absorbing the craft in the company of more-experienced peers. If those opportunities become scarcer, the deeper consequences may not become apparent for years. Software organizations may yet discover that generating code is easier than developing the people who can make sense of it.
