item.title: ‘The Math is Not Fair’
item.dc:creator: Leah Hoffmann
item.description: "Limiting the algorithmic use of data when it’s to our advantage is not necessary."
item.content:encoded:
With a master’s degree in journalism and a Ph.D. in computer science, Simson Garfinkel has had an unusual career—befitting his interests at the intersection of AI, privacy, and digital forensics. Currently chief scientist and chief operating officer of startup accelerator BasisTech and an adjunct lecturer in public policy at Harvard University, Garfinkel is active on the ACM Global Technology Policy Council,a as well as the ACM Publications Board’s Ethics and Plagiarism Committee.b Here, we talk to him about privacy, policy, and how to teach programming in the age of AI vibe coding.

Let’s start with your work on differential privacy, which is a set of methods for protecting the confidential data that are used in public statistics.

Differential privacy marks an evolution in roughly 80 years of research in how to publish statistics that are based on data about individuals, without revealing information about those individuals.

You led the deployment of differential privacy in the 2020 U.S. Census, and you’ve written a book about the topic.c

I was a differential privacy skeptic when I showed up at the Census Bureau. I wanted there to be an alternative, but I never found it. The problem is, the math is not fair. People would really like to live in a world where you can publish highly accurate data about individuals and not violate the privacy of those individuals, and that’s just not the world that we live in.

Yet there are techniques for making tradeoffs between privacy and statistical accuracy.

One of the challenges is that, before the invention of differential privacy, the policy makers didn’t want to deal with that tradeoff, so they just handed it to the statisticians. And the statisticians, for the most part, assumed that there was a correct tradeoff, and it was a purely technical question. Then, in the late 1990s and early 2000s, computer scientists discovered—and it really was a discovery—that it wasn’t a purely technical question, that there was no ‘right’ setting, and that there would always be a tradeoff between privacy loss and accuracy. They said, “This is great. We have a mechanism, and now the policy makers can actually make policy.”

I hesitate to ask how that went in the case of your work on the Census.

Differential privacy allows data to be tuned for specific applications and not tuned for other applications, because you can control where the uncertainty appears. If you’re interested in using statistics to distribute federal funds by county, you can tune the results so that the data are very good for doing that, but not good for, say, doing block-by-block gerrymandering. I can’t speak to what the Census Bureau did, because those decisions were made after I left. But certainly an actor that wanted to use Census data for specific applications might not want the data to be tuned to support other ones.

You’ve written extensively about tech-related policies through the ACM d and in other outlets, where you’re frank about these types of tradeoffs and how they play out in the public sphere.

I try to write about policy issues from a policy-neutral point of view. That doesn’t mean that I give people the facts and let them make up their minds, because that doesn’t work very well. Instead, what I try to do is to give people the facts and outline the decision space and what the implications are of different choices. I try to be fair to viewpoints that are not intentionally inflammatory, though one of the challenges we’ve had in computer science lately is that some topics that were not politically charged have become politically charged.

Please explain.

The way that words are used is a challenge. In statistics and machine learning, terms such as “discriminant” have long been used to describe methods that separate populations. Today, we need to be more specific and deliberate in our choice of words, in part because we need to pay attention to what our methods are actually doing. For example, in lending, we need to be sure that we are evaluating a person’s ability and willingness to repay a loan, rather than basing an analysis on a proxy variable that might combine repayment risk with a factor that is legally and ethically impermissible to use, such as a person’s race or heritage.

I imagine there’s a similar dynamic in the world of privacy.

Daniel Solove has a taxonomy of privacy that I highly recommend. We use the word “privacy” to mean both “free from intrusion” and also to control the distribution of private information about ourselves. We seem to think it’s pro-privacy to limit the algorithmic use of personal data when the way that it’s used is to our detriment. But limiting the algorithmic use of data when it’s to our advantage is not necessary.

In other words, it’s not a privacy problem if my transaction history is used to give me discounts at the store, but it is a problem if it’s used to give me higher prices.

From a math point of view, it’s the same use of personal data. It’s just whether or not I’m benefiting.

Let’s change course for a bit and talk about AI. I was intrigued by your recent suggestion that we should flip the way we teach computer programming.

Currently, we teach programming from the bottom up, starting with syntax and variables and loops and “if” statements. Before that, we used to start with flowcharts and assembly language. It’s an open question whether that’s the right way to teach people to program. If I’m designing a program to do something fairly sophisticated, I don’t approach it from the bottom up—I approach it from the top down.

But isn’t that an expert’s approach, honed after years and years of engaging with low-level details?

Right now, people are describing the program they want and an LLM is stamping out code, and it’s working. Maybe it’s doing something that’s not quite what they want, so they describe changes and they iterate. They have to think logically about what the program should do and the possible failure cases, they have to test it and, if it doesn’t work the first time, they have to debug it. I believe that’s going to be the way most people on this planet are programming in two years. Not most programmers today, but most people who are programming.

Thinking logically about a program’s function and specifications is certainly part of computing, though it’s hard to see how you could reach an especially sophisticated understanding if you never engage with actual code.

So, our field already went through this when compilers became readily available. Back in the 1950s, people thought that you had to learn assembler. And then at some point, I think in the 1980s, they stopped teaching assembler—though when I was an undergraduate at MIT, it was still the case that everybody had to take a course about machine code. People don’t learn machine code anymore, generally.

It’s a worthy historical point.

There’s an underappreciation of computer science history in the field, in particular, an underappreciation of how useful it is. It’s common to see Ph.D. students spend a few days solving a problem that someone else spent two or three years thinking about. Usually, the old solution took things into account that aren’t issues for today’s computers. But there are almost always aspects—clever things that were done, ways of representing data—that the person who ran it off in three days could have benefited from learning.

Now, when the LLMs write code, you would hope they would take all that history into account, but it doesn’t seem that they do. They are lazy, just like a lot of graduate students are lazy. They really don’t want to do that literature search.

That’s strangely relatable. LLMs: they’re just like us!

It is so much easier to write something new than to inventory what has come before. It’s a problem for us as a field.

item.title: ACM Global Engagement Board: Vision and Mission
item.dc:creator: George Neville-Neil and Maria Soledad Pera
item.description: The board's mandate is both simple and ambitious: to expand ACM’s global reach and support computing professionals irrespective of geographic location.
item.content:encoded:
Computing is inherently global. The systems we build, the challenges we address, and the communities we serve transcend geographic boundaries. As the largest computing society bringing together computing educators, researchers, and professionals, the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM)a has the mandate to advance computing as a science and profession for the benefit of all. Yet, while computing is everywhere, participation remains uneven. Access, infrastructure, language, and opportunity still shape who can take part—and who cannot. If computing is to meet the world’s most urgent and complex challenges, more must be done to ensure inclusion is not only an aspiration, but a reality.

The creation of the ACM Global Engagement Board marks an important step in this direction. The Board is the direct outcome of a Presidential Task Force established in 2024, followed by a global survey designed to surface needs, barriers, and opportunities across regions. The findings were clear: Regional realities differ significantly, and meaningful engagement requires understanding those differences and acting on them. The recommendation that emerged was equally clear: the need for a dedicated structure within ACM to sustain and coordinate global engagement.

Our mandate is both simple and ambitious: to expand ACM’s global reach and support computing professionals irrespective of geographic location. This includes advancing inclusivity, increasing regional participation, strengthening connections between academia and industry, and enhancing ACM’s local visibility through culturally and contextually relevant initiatives. Central to this mandate is the generation of accurate, on-the-ground insights (grounded in the lived realities of diverse communities) to inform ACM’s broader global strategy while reinforcing long-term volunteer engagement.

Global engagement must be built from the ground up—anchored in regional insight, shaped by local communities, and informed by existing infrastructure. Regional communities best understand their own needs, constraints, and opportunities. The Board’s role is not to reinvent the wheel, but to connect and enable existing efforts: to amplify what works and to facilitate the cross-pollination of ideas across ACM’s ecosystem. In doing so, it draws on the considerable strengths already present in ACM Special Interest Groups (SIGs), councils, and other ACM entities, ensuring lessons learned in one context can inform progress in another.

Our philosophy is reflected in the Board’s composition. As co-chairs of the Global Engagement Board, we work alongside a globally representative group of leaders. Regional Committees have been established across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. These committees are led by Anicia Peters (Africa), Kian Lee Tan (Asia), Altigran Soares da Silva (Latin America and the Caribbean), and Indira R. Guzman (North America). Leadership from ACM’s established Councils, including Rosa M. Badia (Europe), Meenakshi D’Souza (India), and Huadong Ma (China), are also part of the board. Each Committee and Council brings together a broad set of volunteers, ensuring diverse perspectives inform both regional initiatives and ACM’s global direction. In addition, the Board benefits from the contributions of Members-at-Large Fabrizio Gagliardi and Phillip Paeps. Collectively, the Board reflects the geographic and professional diversity that defines computing today.

The Board’s vision is rooted in a simple but powerful idea: belonging. No one should need to travel to a particular place to feel they are part of the computing community, nor depend on access to a limited set of geographic or institutional resources to participate meaningfully. The most impactful solutions are often developed locally, by those who understand their contexts deeply. ACM’s role is to enable this work—to lower barriers, foster connections, and ensure access, participation, and opportunity are equitably distributed worldwide.

Realizing this vision requires action that is both locally grounded and globally connected. Regional committees will engage with existing organizations, foster partnerships, and support the growth of ACM chapters where they are most needed. They will help adapt membership models to regional contexts, expand multilingual resources, and broaden access to training and professional development. Listening remains central to this process. Through ongoing surveys and sustained regional engagement, the Board will continue to build a nuanced understanding of evolving needs—ensuring ACM’s global strategy remains responsive, evidence-based, and inclusive.

Just as important as what the Board does is what it does not seek to do. It is not meant to centralize effort or duplicate existing work. Rather, it acts as a connective layer, linking regions, initiatives, and communities; enabling collaboration; and amplifying impact. Its purpose is to help ACM better serve practitioners and researchers everywhere by becoming more attuned to local realities while strengthening global cohesion.

The path of global engagement for ACM will be iterative and collective. Building an even more global and inclusive computing community will require sustained effort, open dialogue, and active participation from across ACM and beyond. We invite ACM members, volunteers, and partners to engage with the Global Engagement Board—whether by contributing ideas, participating in regional efforts, or sharing experiences that can help guide this evolving initiative. More information about the Board and its activities can be found on ACM’s Global Engagement Board’s webpage.b

Computing does not happen in isolation; it happens everywhere. ACM must lead by working alongside the communities it serves. A more inclusive, more connected, and more representative ACM is not optional; it is a responsibility, and one we must fulfill together. This is the way to a computing community without borders.

item.title: In Memoriam: Richard A. Tapia (1939-2026)
item.dc:creator: Eugene H. Spafford and Simson L. Garfinkel
item.description: Tapia described his work using a single sentence: "I have to serve as a role model by first being an excellent scientist."
item.content:encoded:
It is unusual for living computer scientists to have a conference named after them; Richard Alfred Tapia had two. The ACM Richard Tapia Celebration of Diversity in Computing draws thousands every year. The Blackwell-Tapia Conference, held biennially since 2000, honors Tapia jointly with the late statistician David Blackwell—recognizing both as eminent mathematicians and as sustained advocates for African-American, Latino, and Native American scholars in the mathematical sciences. Both conferences were established during Tapia’s career by colleagues who believed his scholarship and mentorship deserved institutional recognition. Tapia, the Maxfield and Oshman University Professor at Rice University, died on May 22, 2026, in Houston, TX, at the age of 87.

Tapia was a numerical optimization researcher and a noted mentor who lived those two careers as one. President Barack Obama presented him with the National Medal of Science in 2011 “for his pioneering and fundamental contributions in optimization theory and numerical analysis and for his dedication and sustained efforts in fostering diversity and excellence in mathematics and science education.” The citation deliberately tied the two tracks together; Tapia had been saying for decades that they were inseparable.

Born in Santa Monica, CA, to Amado Bernal Tapia and Maria Magdalena Angulo Tapia on March 25, 1939, Richard was one of five children and the first in his family to attend college. His parents emigrated separately from Mexico as impoverished young people seeking education, but both ended up working rather than completing school. Not so for their children: four of the five earned undergraduate degrees, and three earned graduate degrees. 

“So the roles that I identify with and make me happy are: Chicano, Tejano, mathematician, and car enthusiast,” Tapia wrote in his contribution to the Mathematical Association of America’s Testimonios. 

That fourth identity—car enthusiast—was not a throwaway. He and his twin brother Bobby were drag racers from age 15; in 1968, the brothers set a world record in elapsed time for fuel dragster racing, traveling a quarter mile in 6.54 seconds. Bobby was inducted into the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) Hall of Fame in 2002. Richard restored classic cars and exhibited a custom 1970 Chevelle that earned first-in-class awards at the Houston AutoRama and the San Antonio car show. He joined his two passions in a lecture, “Math at Top Speed: Exploring and Breaking Myths in the Drag Racing Folklore,” delivered at universities and mathematics-awareness events for decades.

Tapia won the local American Mathematical Society math contest the year he graduated from high school, but his school never gave him the assembly recognition that had been promised. He worked in a muffler factory after graduation. A co-worker from Mississippi, whose own schooling had stopped early, told him, “Richard, do not make my mistake. You are smart, go to college.” That September, Tapia enrolled at Harbor Junior College in Wilmington, where a calculus professor urged him to attend the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) rather than a state school. There, he earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics in 1961 and took a job at Todd Shipyards in San Pedro, working on a Navy grant to define ship hull surfaces. 

Tapia returned to UCLA for graduate study in 1963 and worked part-time at IBM Westwood, earning his master’s degree in 1966 and his Ph.D. in 1967. His dissertation, “A Generalization of Newton’s Method with an Application to the Euler-Lagrange Equation,” established the territory he would work in for the rest of his career.

After a year at UCLA as an instructor, Tapia spent 1968 to 1970 as a postdoctoral fellow at the Army Mathematics Research Center at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He joined Rice University in 1970, was tenured in 1972, and was promoted to full professor in 1976. He chaired the Department of Mathematical Sciences from 1978 to 1983. In 1991, he was named the Noah Harding Professor of Computational and Applied Mathematics; in 2005, he was named the Maxfield and Oshman Professor of Engineering and a University Professor—Rice’s highest academic honor.

Tapia’s research portfolio included nonlinear iterative methods, trust-region methods for unconstrained optimization, sequential quadratic programming, interior-point methods for linear and nonlinear programming, and nonparametric density and function estimation. He wrote two books with James R. Thompson: Nonparametric Probability Density Estimation (Johns Hopkins, 1978) and Nonparametric Function Estimation, Modeling, and Simulation (SIAM, 1990). He authored or co-authored more than 100 research papers. He served as editor of SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis (1978–1991), the Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications (1981–1996), and SIAM Journal on Optimization (1990–1991). He supervised 38 doctoral students, and his academic descendants are present in numerical optimization research groups across the U.S. and Latin America.

In talks and interviews across four decades, Tapia described his work using a single sentence: “I have to serve as a role model by first being an excellent scientist.” Excellence in the discipline was the precondition for the mentorship mission. He believed the field would not open itself to students from underrepresented communities until they saw researchers from those communities doing first-rate technical work. Therefore, he insisted on doing it himself.

ACM Fellow and Rice faculty colleague Moshe Y. Vardi observed, “Two things stood out to me about my colleague and friend, Richard Tapia: He was committed to the idea that the purpose of science is betterment of the world, and he did not hesitate to take an even broader perspective on that goal; and when he gave talks, either about diversity or about math, it was not some abstract academic who was giving the talk. It was always a very personal talk.”

Tapia acted on this belief at every scale. In 1972, his second year at Rice, he founded the Rice Association of Mexican-American Students (RAMAS) and became a founding member of the Society for the Advancement of Chicanos and Native Americans in Science (SACNAS), whose 1973 inaugural meeting in Atlantic City drew 50 young Chicano and Native scientists. He later founded the Tapia Center at Rice, which has grown into a hub for outreach programs, including the Tapia STEM Camps for talented 8th- through 12th-graders. This effort grew from roughly 40 participants in 2015 to more than 1,200 by 2025. He directed the NSF-supported Alliance for Graduate Education and the Professoriate for more than a decade, founded Rice’s Graduate Education for Minorities and its Empowering Leadership Alliance programs, and founded Rice’s President’s Lecture Series of Diverse Scholars. The Tapia Conference biography summarized the cumulative effect: “He has directed or co-directed more underrepresented minority and women doctoral recipients in science and engineering than anyone in the country.”

The first Tapia Celebration of Diversity in Computing, sponsored by ACM and organized by the Coalition to Diversify Computing, drew 164 attendees in Houston in 2001. Now run by the Center for Minorities and People with Disabilities in Information Technology (CMD-IT), it is the principal venue where the American computing community visibly does the work Tapia had been doing individually for 30 years. The Blackwell-Tapia Mathematics Conference plays the same role for the mathematical sciences.

“I first met Richard when my mother and I visited Rice after I was accepted for grad school,” said Illya Hicks, professor and department chair of CMOR at Rice. “We knocked on his office door and spent about an hour and a half with him. He immediately enrolled me in his Spend a Summer with a Scientist program. When we were ready to leave, he told my mother, ‘We will take good care of your son.’ That statement perfectly describes how Richard treated every student he encountered. It is because of his mentorship that I am a professor today.”

Valerie Taylor, ACM Fellow and president and CEO of CMD-IT, summarized the reach of his career: “Richard Tapia has had a major impact on the computing community through his research in optimization, his advocacy for increasing diversity in STEM, his tireless effort to change policy through his service on boards, such as the National Science Board, and his personal outreach to strengthen the community.”

Tapia was the first U.S.-born Hispanic person elected to the National Academy of Engineering (1992), the first mathematician to hold the title of University Professor at Rice (and the sixth person in the university’s then-94-year history to do so), and the first recipient of the Computing Research Association’s A. Nico Habermann Award (1994). About two months before he died, the Harris County Commissioners voted unanimously to rename the Sam Houston Tollway Ship Channel Bridge in his honor.

He served on the National Science Board from 1996 to 2002 and chaired the National Research Council’s Board on Higher Education and the Workforce from 2001 to 2004. He was on the SIAM Board of Trustees from 1989 to 1992. He received the NSF’s inaugural Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring in 1996; the AAAS Lifetime Mentor Award in 1998; the SIAM Distinguished Service to the Profession Award and the AMS Distinguished Public Service Award in 2004; the National Medal of Science in 2011; the National Science Board’s Vannevar Bush Award in 2014; the AAAS Public Engagement with Science Award in 2016; and was elected as a Fellow of the American Mathematical Society in 2021. He received eight honorary doctorates. 

Tapia was predeceased by his daughter, Circee Lynn Tapia, in 1982; his sister, Ana, in 2009; his twin brother, Robert (Bobby), in April 2020; and his wife, Jean Rodriguez Tapia, in November 2022, after 63 years of marriage. He is survived by his son, Richard (Rich) Amado Tapia; his daughter, Rebecca (Becky) Anna Tapia; his sister, Rebecca Amelia Tapia; and his brother, Steven (Steve) Paul Tapia.
